topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10 using objects or drawings
evidence: Solve 'There are 6 apples, 2 are eaten, how many left?' using counters
Solve 'add to' and 'take from' result-unknown problems
Solve 'put together/take apart' problems with total unknown
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'There are 7 birds on a fence and 3 fly away — how many are left?', can {{name}} work it out using their fingers, counters, or a quick drawing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition as combining or putting together two
topics.description: Understand addition as combining or putting together two groups to find the total
evidence: Model 'putting together' with physical objects and say the total
Act out an 'add to' situation (e.g. 3 children arrive, then 2 more join)
Explain that addition means finding how many altogether
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 4 toy cars and a friend brings 3 more, do they understand that adding means combining both groups — and can they tell you there are now 7 cars altogether?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number bonds to 9
topics.description: Find the number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9 (number bonds to 10)
evidence: Given 7, respond '3' to make 10
Use a ten-frame to find the complement to 10
Record pairs that make 10 as equations (e.g. 6 + 4 = 10)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and needs 10 for a recipe, can they quickly tell you they need 4 more — without counting all the way up from 1?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers up to 10 into pairs
topics.description: Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way (part-part-whole)
evidence: Use objects or drawings to find all pairs that make a given number
Record decompositions as equations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 8 grapes, can they split them into two groups in different ways — like 3 and 5, or 4 and 4 — and explain that both groups together still make 8?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Representing Addition and Subtraction
topics.description: Represent addition and subtraction using objects, drawings, and mental images
evidence: Use cubes or counters to show 3 + 2
Draw a picture to represent a subtraction situation
Use fingers to model an addition problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 3 apples and you give them 2 more, can they show you how many there are altogether — using their fingers, some small objects, or a drawing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Subtraction as taking away or separating
topics.description: Understand subtraction as taking away or separating from a group to find how many remain
evidence: Model 'taking away' with physical objects and say how many remain
Act out a 'take from' situation (e.g. 5 biscuits, eat 2, how many left?)
Explain that subtraction means finding how many are left
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 9 biscuits and eats 3, do they understand that subtracting means taking some away — and can they tell you 6 biscuits are left?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting
topics.description: Add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero
evidence: Calculate 14 + 5 = 19
Calculate 17 – 3 = 14
Add or subtract 0 and explain the result stays the same
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '14 + 5' or '18 − 6' in their head or on paper, and do they know that adding or taking away zero leaves the number unchanged?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Early Word Problems
topics.description: Solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems
evidence: Solve 'I have 12 sweets and eat 4, how many left?'
Solve missing number: 7 = [ ] – 9
Solve problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'I had some sweets, ate 5, and now have 9 left — how many did I start with?', can {{name}} figure out the missing number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 5
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 5
evidence: Answer 2 + 3 quickly without counting on fingers
Answer 5 – 2 from recall or with minimal counting
Complete a set of within-5 addition/subtraction facts accurately and quickly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give you the answer to sums like '2 + 3' or '5 − 2' straight away, without needing to count on their fingers every time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number bonds
topics.description: Recall number bonds (addition and related subtraction facts) within 20
evidence: Quickly recall that 8 + 5 = 13
Given 13 – 5, respond 8 using knowledge of related addition fact
Know all pairs of single-digit numbers that sum to numbers up to 20
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts like '8 + 7 = 15' and immediately know that '15 − 7 = 8' — without having to work out the subtraction from scratch?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading +, −, and = symbols
topics.description: Read, write, and interpret the symbols +, −, and = in number sentences
evidence: Read 3 + 2 = 5 aloud as 'three plus two equals five'
Write a number sentence to match a concrete addition situation
Interpret the = sign as 'is the same as' rather than just 'the answer is'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you write '4 + 3 = 7' on paper, can {{name}} tell you what the plus sign, minus sign, and equals sign each mean?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting tens mentally
topics.description: Add and subtract a two-digit number and tens mentally and using concrete/pictorial representations
evidence: Calculate 45 + 30 = 75 mentally
Calculate 82 − 40 = 42 mentally
Explain that only the tens digit changes when adding/subtracting tens
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '54 + 30' or '78 − 20' in their head — knowing that only the tens digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Three Small Numbers
topics.description: Add three one-digit numbers using strategies including looking for pairs that make 10
evidence: Calculate 5 + 7 + 3 by first adding 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15
Add any three single-digit numbers correctly
Identify useful pairs within three addends to make the calculation easier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 4 + 6 + 8, can they spot that 4 and 6 make 10 first, then add 8 to get 18 — rather than just adding in order from left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding two two-digit numbers
topics.description: Add and subtract two two-digit numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mental methods
evidence: Calculate 34 + 27 using base-ten blocks or column addition
Calculate 63 − 28 using a number line or partitioning
Explain a strategy for adding or subtracting two two-digit numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract two two-digit numbers — like '43 + 28' — using counters, a drawing, or working it out in their head?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding within 100
topics.description: Add within 100 using strategies based on place value, including adding a two-digit and one-digit number, and a two-digit and a multiple of 10
evidence: Calculate 46 + 7 using place value (46 + 4 + 3 = 53)
Calculate 38 + 40 = 78 using tens understanding
Relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '47 + 8' or '35 + 50' by thinking about the tens and ones separately rather than counting up one at a time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies
topics.description: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction
evidence: Add 8 + 3 by starting at 8 and counting on 3 (9, 10, 11)
Subtract 12 − 3 by counting back 3 from 12 (11, 10, 9)
Explain that counting on is a way to add
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '8 + 5', can they start from 8 and count up five more — rather than starting from 1 every time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction within 20
topics.description: Add and subtract within 20 using strategies such as making ten, decomposing a number leading to ten, and using known facts
evidence: Solve 8 + 6 using making ten: 8 + 2 + 4 = 14
Solve 13 − 4 by decomposing: 13 − 3 − 1 = 9
Use a known fact (8 + 4 = 12) to derive 12 − 8 = 4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '8 + 6', can they split the 6 into 2 + 4, use the 2 to fill up to 10, then add the remaining 4 to get 14?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition in any order
topics.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of addition: addends can be added in any order
evidence: Explain that 3 + 8 gives the same answer as 8 + 3
Use commutativity to choose the larger number to count on from
Demonstrate that subtraction is not commutative (5 − 3 ≠ 3 − 5)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that 6 + 4 gives the same answer as 4 + 6, so they can always choose whichever order makes the adding easier?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding a missing number in addition
topics.description: Understand subtraction as finding an unknown addend (e.g. 10 − 8 = ? is the same as 8 + ? = 10)
evidence: Solve 10 − 8 by thinking 'what do I add to 8 to make 10?'
Explain that subtraction can be thought of as a missing-addend problem
Use known addition facts to solve related subtraction problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} see that '10 − 8 = ?' is the same as asking 'what do I add to 8 to reach 10?' — so they can use their adding knowledge to help with subtraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 10
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 10
evidence: Answer any addition fact within 10 quickly from memory
Answer any subtraction fact within 10 quickly from memory
Complete a timed set of within-10 facts with high accuracy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} answer sums like '7 + 3' or '9 − 4' almost instantly — without stopping to count on their fingers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent addition and subtraction
topics.description: Recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100
evidence: Rapidly recall 7 + 8 = 15 and 15 − 8 = 7
Use 6 + 4 = 10 to derive 60 + 40 = 100
Derive 35 + 5 = 40 from knowledge that 5 + 5 = 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts like '9 + 7 = 16' and '16 − 7 = 9', and use those to help work out bigger sums like '90 + 70'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Grouping numbers to add
topics.description: Understand and apply the associative property of addition: when adding three numbers, any two can be added first
evidence: Solve 2 + 6 + 4 by first adding 6 + 4 = 10, then 2 + 10 = 12
Explain that grouping addends differently gives the same total
Choose which two numbers to add first to make the calculation easier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 3 + 7 + 6, can they spot that adding 3 and 7 first (to make 10) is easier — rather than always working left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Inverse: addition undoes subtraction
topics.description: Recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems
evidence: Check 15 + 7 = 22 by calculating 22 − 7 = 15
Use the inverse to solve: □ + 9 = 14, so □ = 14 − 9 = 5
Explain that addition and subtraction 'undo' each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out 13 + 5 = 18, can they immediately use that to say '18 − 5 = 13' — without having to work the subtraction out all over again?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 6+)
topics.description: Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones mentally and using concrete/pictorial representations
evidence: Calculate 36 + 7 = 43 using objects or mentally
Calculate 52 − 4 = 48 using a number line or mentally
Explain bridging through 10 when adding ones to a two-digit number
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '36 + 7' or '42 − 5' in their head — keeping the tens in place and only adjusting the ones?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental and written addition and subtraction
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems using mental and written methods, including problems involving numbers, quantities, and measures
evidence: Solve a two-step problem: 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p. How much now?'
Choose an appropriate method (mental or written) for a given problem
Solve problems involving measures, e.g. 'a ribbon is 45cm, I cut off 18cm'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a problem involving lengths, weights, or prices, can they decide whether to add or subtract and carry out the calculation correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Subtracting multiples of 10
topics.description: Subtract multiples of 10 (10–90) from multiples of 10 using place value strategies
evidence: Calculate 70 − 30 = 40
Use base-ten blocks to show 80 − 50 = 30
Explain that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '80 − 50' or '70 − 40' in their head by thinking about how many tens are left?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unknown in Addition & Subtraction
topics.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers
evidence: Solve 8 + ? = 11 and write 3
Solve 5 = □ − 3 and write 8
Solve 6 + 6 = □ and write 12
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees '? + 6 = 14' or '9 − ? = 4' written on paper, can they figure out what number goes in the gap?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What the equals sign means
topics.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign as 'is the same as' and determine if equations are true or false
evidence: Explain that 6 = 6 is true because both sides are the same
Determine that 4 + 1 = 5 + 2 is false
Understand that = does not mean 'the answer comes next' — it means balance
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that '=' means 'the same as', so they can tell you whether '4 + 3 = 8 − 1' is true or false?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 7+)
topics.description: Add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction
evidence: Set out a columnar addition correctly with digits aligned by place value
Carry out columnar subtraction with exchange (borrowing) when needed
Check the answer using the inverse operation or estimation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} set out a sum like '347 + 265' or '512 − 278' in columns and work through it step by step, carrying or borrowing where needed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding numbers
topics.description: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations
evidence: Add three or four two-digit numbers by grouping tens and ones
Look for pairs that make multiples of 10 to simplify addition
Explain the strategy used to combine multiple addends
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add up four two-digit numbers — like '14 + 23 + 32 + 19' — by grouping them cleverly, rather than just plodding through from left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies (age 7+)
topics.description: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations
evidence: Explain why adding tens and ones separately gives the correct total
Describe why a compensation strategy works (e.g. 'I added 1 too many, so I subtract 1')
Use place-value language to justify a written method step by step
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out '67 + 24' by splitting it into '60 + 20' and '7 + 4', can they explain to you in words *why* that approach gives the right answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction within 1000
topics.description: Add and subtract within 1000 using concrete models, drawings, and strategies based on place value; understand composing and decomposing tens and hundreds
evidence: Add two three-digit numbers using base-ten blocks or drawings, composing a ten or hundred when necessary
Subtract three-digit numbers, decomposing a ten or hundred when necessary
Relate the concrete/drawn strategy to a written method and explain why it works
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract numbers in the hundreds — like '347 + 256' — by thinking about hundreds, tens, and ones separately, or drawing a diagram to help?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating by rounding
topics.description: Estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers; apply to increasingly large numbers using rounding and inverse reasoning
evidence: Round numbers to the nearest 10 or 100 to estimate a sum or difference before calculating
Use addition to check a subtraction answer, or vice versa
Identify when a calculated answer is unreasonable based on the estimate
Round numbers to estimate a sum or difference before calculating
Use addition to check a subtraction answer and vice versa
Identify an unreasonable answer by comparing to the estimate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} works out a calculation, can they make a sensible rough guess — and then check their answer using the opposite operation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 100
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction
evidence: Add two-digit numbers within 100 efficiently (e.g. 46 + 37 using place-value partitioning)
Subtract two-digit numbers within 100 fluently (e.g. 83 − 25)
Choose between strategies (decomposing, compensating, using known facts) based on the numbers involved
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} reliably add or subtract two-digit numbers like '68 + 27' or '91 − 45', choosing the best strategy for each problem?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 20
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers
evidence: Answer any single-digit addition fact within 3 seconds
Recall subtraction facts within 20 from memory (e.g. 15 − 8 = 7)
Use known addition facts to derive related subtraction facts rapidly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} instantly recall all the single-digit addition facts — like '7 + 8 = 15' — without needing to count or think for more than a second?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 7+)
topics.description: Mentally add and subtract a three-digit number and ones
evidence: Calculate 345 + 7 mentally
Calculate 462 − 5 mentally
Explain that only the ones digit changes (unless bridging through a ten)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '436 + 7' or '521 − 8' in their head — keeping the hundreds and tens unchanged while adjusting just the ones?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mentally adding hundreds to 3-digit numbers
topics.description: Mentally add and subtract a three-digit number and hundreds
evidence: Calculate 345 + 200 mentally
Calculate 762 − 400 mentally
Explain that only the hundreds digit changes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '342 + 200' or '756 − 300' in their head — knowing that only the hundreds digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mentally adding tens to 3-digit numbers
topics.description: Mentally add and subtract a three-digit number and tens
evidence: Calculate 345 + 40 mentally
Calculate 462 − 30 mentally
Explain that only the tens digit changes (unless bridging through a hundred)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '354 + 40' or '628 − 30' in their head — knowing that only the tens digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Missing number problems (age 7+)
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems including missing-number problems, using number facts, place value, and more complex methods
evidence: Solve a missing-number problem such as 245 + ? = 380
Choose an appropriate method (mental, written, or combination) based on the numbers
Solve multi-step problems combining addition and subtraction of three-digit numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums with a hidden number — like '? − 38 = 24' or '53 + ? = 91' — by thinking carefully about what the equation is asking?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Represent whole numbers as lengths on a number line and represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram
evidence: Place whole numbers on a number line with equally spaced points
Show an addition as a jump forward on the number line (e.g. 38 + 27 shown as jumps)
Show a subtraction as a jump backward on the number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} mark numbers on a number line and show what happens when they add or subtract — for example, jumping forward 35 places from 48?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two-Step Word Problems
topics.description: Solve one- and two-step word problems within 100 using addition and subtraction, with unknowns in all positions
evidence: Solve a two-step word problem involving adding to and taking from
Represent a word problem with an equation using a symbol for the unknown
Solve comparison problems (how many more/fewer) within 100
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a word problem says 'Sam had 78 stickers, gave some away, and now has 45 — how many did he give away?', can {{name}} work out which operation to use and find the answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 8+)
topics.description: Add and subtract numbers with up to four digits using formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction
evidence: Set out and solve a columnar addition with up to four-digit numbers
Set out and solve a columnar subtraction with exchange across multiple columns
Check the answer using estimation or inverse operations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} line up a sum like '3,842 + 1,765' or '4,301 − 2,658' in columns and work through it correctly — carrying and borrowing across multiple columns?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 1000
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction
evidence: Add two three-digit numbers fluently using an efficient method
Subtract three-digit numbers fluently, including with regrouping
Choose the most efficient strategy based on the numbers involved
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract three-digit numbers like '672 − 348' reliably, choosing whichever method works best for them?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two-step addition and subtraction problems
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why
evidence: Identify the two steps needed to solve a contextual problem
Choose between mental and written methods for each step based on the numbers
Explain why the chosen operations and methods are appropriate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a word problem with two steps — like working out change from a shopping trip with two items — can they plan which calculations to do and in what order?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two-Step Equations
topics.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations; represent problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity
evidence: Solve a two-step problem that combines addition/subtraction with multiplication/division
Write an equation using a letter for the unknown (e.g. 3 × n + 5 = 26)
Assess the reasonableness of the answer using estimation and mental computation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write an equation like 'n + 25 = 60' to represent a word problem, and then solve it to find what n equals?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why
evidence: A school collects 12,450 bottles in Week 1 and 8,372 in Week 2; their target is 25,000 — how many more do they need?
Choose between mental and written methods for each step and explain why
Solve a three-step problem involving addition and subtraction of five-digit numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a multi-step problem — like planning a budget where money is added and spent in several steps — can they decide which operations to use at each stage and explain their thinking?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Checking Answers by Rounding
topics.description: Use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine appropriate levels of accuracy in context
evidence: Check 47,832 + 23,156 ≈ 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000 to verify the exact answer 70,988
Decide whether to round to the nearest 100 or 1,000 for a given estimation context
Identify that a calculated answer of 3,421 cannot be correct because the estimate gives approximately 50,000
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets an answer of 4,213 for an addition, can they round the numbers to double-check — like '4,000 + 1,000 ≈ 5,000' — and spot if the answer seems way off?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent addition and subtraction (age 9+)
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract whole numbers with more than four digits using the standard columnar algorithm
evidence: Calculate 34,567 + 28,945 using columnar addition
Calculate 500,000 − 234,178 using columnar subtraction with multiple exchanges
Add three five-digit numbers in a single column layout
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} accurately add or subtract large numbers — like '23,846 + 14,579' — using the column method, carrying and borrowing correctly however many columns it takes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 9+)
topics.description: Add and subtract numbers mentally with increasingly large numbers, using place-value knowledge and derived facts
evidence: Mentally calculate 45,000 + 8,000
Mentally subtract 3,200 from 10,000 by counting up
Use near-doubles: 2,500 + 2,600 = 5,100
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out something like '4,700 − 1,300' in their head using what they know about place value — without needing to write it all out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 10+)
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals
evidence: Solve a two-step word problem involving addition and subtraction of numbers beyond 1,000,000
Choose between mental, written, and calculator methods for a multi-step problem and justify the choice
Interpret a real-life context to identify which addition/subtraction operations are needed across multiple steps
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a complicated word problem involving large numbers or decimals — like calculating the total cost of several items — can they plan and carry out all the steps correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies (age 10+)
topics.description: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate strategies to written methods and explain reasoning
evidence: Correctly compute 3.45 + 2.78 and explain regrouping across decimal places
Use a number line or base-ten blocks to model 5.03 − 2.67
Explain why the standard algorithm works for decimal addition by connecting to place-value understanding
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract decimal amounts like '4.73 + 2.68' or '10.00 − 3.47', lining up the decimal points and working through the columns correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Positive and Negative Numbers
topics.description: Understand positive and negative numbers as describing quantities with opposite directions or values; use them in context such as temperature, floors in a building, and bank balances
evidence: Represent positive and negative numbers on a number line and explain what zero means in context
Add a positive or negative number to any integer using number line reasoning
Subtract a positive or negative number from any integer, understanding that subtracting a negative is equivalent to adding
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees temperatures like −3°C and +5°C on a weather forecast, can they figure out how much warmer one day is than the other — even when the answer crosses zero?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equations with Two Unknowns
topics.description: Find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with two unknowns (e.g. find pairs (a, b) where a + b = 10 or 2a + b = 15)
evidence: List all whole-number pairs (a, b) where a + b = 12 with a, b > 0
Find three pairs that satisfy 2x + y = 20
Explain systematically how to generate all integer solutions to a two-variable equation within a given range
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find different pairs of numbers that both satisfy a rule — for example, all the pairs of whole numbers that add up to 10?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Linear number sequences
topics.description: Generate and describe linear number sequences, including those with negative and decimal steps; identify the term-to-term rule
evidence: Continue the sequence 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, ... and state the rule as 'add 1.5'
Generate terms of a sequence that crosses zero (e.g. 3, 1, −1, −3, ...)
Describe the term-to-term rule for a given linear sequence and predict the 10th term
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a number sequence like 3, 7, 11, 15… can they describe the rule, continue it, and predict what the 10th number will be?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number Pattern Relationships
topics.description: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules; identify relationships between corresponding terms; form ordered pairs and graph them on a coordinate plane
evidence: Generate sequences starting at 0 with rules 'add 3' and 'add 6'; observe terms in one are twice the other
Form ordered pairs from corresponding terms and plot them on a coordinate grid
Explain informally why the relationship between the two sequences holds
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} follow two number patterns at once — for example, "add 2" and "add 4" — pair up the matching terms, and plot those pairs as points on a graph?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Systematic Listing
topics.description: Enumerate possibilities of combinations of two variables systematically (e.g. all ways to choose from a set of options)
evidence: List all possible meal combinations from 3 starters and 4 mains
Organise combinations into a systematic table to ensure none are missed
Explain why the total number of combinations equals the product of the options in each category
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} can choose any combination of 3 T-shirt colours and 2 trouser colours, can they list every possible outfit without missing any or repeating?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using Simple Formulae
topics.description: Use simple formulae expressed in words or symbols to calculate values (e.g. perimeter = 2 × (length + width))
evidence: Substitute values into P = 2(l + w) to find the perimeter of a rectangle
Use the formula for area of a triangle (A = 1/2 × b × h) given base and height values
Interpret a formula expressed in words and use it to compute an output
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told that the perimeter of a rectangle uses the formula perimeter = 2 × (length + width), can they plug in the measurements and work out the answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Writing Algebraic Equations
topics.description: Express missing number problems algebraically using letters for unknowns; translate word problems into equations

Solve a one-step equation such as 3x = 24 and explain the reasoning
Express a word problem as an algebraic equation and find the unknown value
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads "I think of a number, double it, and add 5 to get 17," can they write that as an equation using a letter for the unknown and solve it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Algebraic Notation
topics.description: Use and interpret algebraic notation including: ab for a × b, 3y for y + y + y, a² for a × a, a/b for a ÷ b, coefficients as fractions, and brackets for grouping; read and write algebraic expressions fluently
evidence: Read and interpret expressions using standard algebraic conventions for multiplication, division, and powers
Write algebraic expressions from word descriptions using correct notation

topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} sees something written as "3y" or "a²" in a maths problem, do they know what those shorthand notations mean and can they work with them?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Algebraic Transformations
topics.description: Model situations or procedures by translating them into algebraic expressions or formulae and by using graphs; move between word problems, algebraic representations, tables, and graphical representations
evidence: Translate a word problem or real-world situation into an algebraic expression or formula
Construct a table of values from an algebraic rule
Plot the corresponding graph and interpret it in the context of the problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} take a real-world situation — like a taxi that charges £2 plus £1.50 per mile — and write an algebraic formula for the total cost, then sketch what the graph looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Collecting Like Terms
topics.description: Simplify algebraic expressions by collecting like terms — combine terms with the same variable and power (e.g., 3a + 2b + 5a = 8a + 2b) while maintaining equivalence
evidence: Identify like terms in an algebraic expression
Combine like terms involving positive and negative coefficients
Simplify expressions involving multiple variables and constant terms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an expression like "5a + 3b + 2a," can they simplify it by collecting the like terms to get "7a + 3b"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Coordinates (age 11+)
topics.description: Plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane, using positive and negative x- and y-values to describe positions precisely
evidence: Plot points with negative coordinates accurately in all four quadrants
Identify the quadrant a point belongs to from its coordinate signs
Read coordinates from a graph including fractional and negative values
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} plot a point like (−3, 4) correctly on a coordinate grid and read the coordinates of points in all four quadrants, including negative numbers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Expanding Single Brackets
topics.description: Expand (multiply out) a single term over a bracket using the distributive property, e.g., 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15; expand expressions involving negative multipliers
evidence: Multiply a single positive term over a bracket to expand the expression
Multiply a negative term over a bracket, correctly handling signs
Combine expanding brackets with collecting like terms to simplify fully
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} expand a bracket like 3(2x + 5) by multiplying everything inside, to get 6x + 15?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Expressions & Equations Vocabulary
topics.description: Understand and use the concepts and vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms, and factors; distinguish between an expression (no equals sign), an equation (equals sign), and an inequality (inequality sign)
evidence: Define and distinguish between expression, equation, and inequality
Identify terms, coefficients, and factors in algebraic expressions
Use the vocabulary of algebra precisely in mathematical discussions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the difference between an expression like "3x + 2," an equation like "3x + 2 = 11," and an inequality like "3x + 2 > 11"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Generating Sequences
topics.description: Generate terms of a sequence from a term-to-term rule (e.g., 'add 3 each time') or a position-to-term rule (e.g., '2n + 1'), and identify whether a sequence is arithmetic, geometric, or neither
evidence: Continue a sequence given a term-to-term rule involving addition, subtraction, or multiplication
Generate the first five terms from a position-to-term formula such as 3n − 2
Classify sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio), or other
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out the next few terms of a sequence like 5, 8, 11, 14… and explain whether the rule is "add a fixed number each time" or something else?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Understand inequalities as statements comparing expressions, represent solutions on a number line, and solve simple linear inequalities using the same inverse-operation methods as equations
evidence: Write an inequality from a worded constraint (e.g., 'must be at least 12' → x ≥ 12)
Represent the solution set of an inequality on a number line with open or closed circles
Solve a one-step or two-step inequality such as 3x + 1 < 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} solve an inequality like 2x + 1 < 9, show the answer on a number line, and explain what all the solutions have in common?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Solving Linear Equations
topics.description: Use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including equations that require rearrangement, expanding brackets, and collecting terms on both sides; solve equations with rational number coefficients
evidence: Solve one-step and two-step linear equations in one variable
Solve equations requiring expansion of brackets and collection of like terms
Solve equations with the unknown on both sides and with fractional or negative coefficients
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an equation like 3x + 7 = 22, can they work through the steps to find the value of x?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Substituting into Formulae
topics.description: Substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions including scientific formulae; evaluate expressions by replacing variables with given values and computing the result using correct order of operations
evidence: Substitute positive and negative values into algebraic expressions and evaluate
Substitute values into formulae involving multiple operations and powers
Use correct order of operations when evaluating expressions after substitution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a formula says that the area of a triangle is ½ × base × height, can {{name}} substitute in the measurements and calculate the answer correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factorising Expressions
topics.description: Factorise algebraic expressions by taking out common factors — identify the highest common factor of all terms and write the expression as a product, e.g., 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)
evidence: Identify the highest common factor of all terms in an expression
Write the factorised form as a product of the HCF and a bracket
Check factorisation by expanding the brackets back out
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at an expression like "6x + 9" and rewrite it with the common factor taken out — as "3(2x + 3)"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Linear Function Graphs
topics.description: Recognise that a linear function produces a straight-line graph, understand the relationship between an equation of the form y = mx + c and its graphical representation, and interpret gradient and y-intercept in context
evidence: Explain that changing m in y = mx + c alters the steepness and direction of the line
Identify the y-intercept of a line from its equation and from its graph
Determine whether a given equation will produce a straight line or a curve
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the equation y = 2x + 3, can they explain what the graph will look like — including how steep it is and where it crosses the y-axis?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Nth-Term Rules
topics.description: Find the nth-term expression for an arithmetic sequence by identifying the common difference and the zero-term, and use it to determine any term in the sequence or test whether a given number belongs to the sequence
evidence: Derive the nth-term rule for an arithmetic sequence such as 3, 7, 11, 15, … as 4n − 1
Use an nth-term formula to find the 50th or 100th term without listing all preceding terms
Determine whether a given number (e.g., 99) is a term in a specified arithmetic sequence
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given the sequence 4, 7, 10, 13…, can they find a formula for the nth term — and use it to check whether, say, 100 is in the sequence?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Plotting Linear Graphs
topics.description: Plot linear graphs by generating a table of values, reduce a two-variable linear equation to the form y = mx + c, and calculate gradients from two points on a line
evidence: Generate a table of (x, y) values for a linear equation and plot the points accurately
Rearrange an equation such as 2x + 3y = 12 into the form y = mx + c
Calculate the gradient between two coordinate points using rise over run
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw the graph of a straight line by making a table of values and plotting the points — and work out the gradient from two points on the line?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple formulae
topics.description: Understand and use standard mathematical formulae; rearrange formulae to change the subject, performing inverse operations to isolate a different variable
evidence: Identify the subject of a given formula
Use inverse operations to rearrange a formula to make a different variable the subject
Rearrange formulae involving multiple steps including fractions and powers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a formula gives speed as distance ÷ time, can {{name}} rearrange it to find distance or time when they're the unknowns instead?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating answers (age 13+)
topics.description: Use graphs of linear and quadratic functions to estimate output values for given inputs, find approximate solutions to equations, and interpret graphical information in real-world contexts
evidence: Read off an approximate y-value for a given x from a plotted curve
Find approximate solutions to an equation by identifying where a graph crosses the x-axis or another line
Interpret a real-world graph (e.g., distance–time) to answer contextual questions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a graph — whether a straight line or a curve — to read off an answer to an equation approximately, rather than solving it algebraically?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Expanding Double Brackets
topics.description: Expand products of two or more binomials, e.g., (x + 3)(x - 2) = x² + x - 6, using the grid method or FOIL; simplify the result by collecting like terms
evidence: Expand the product of two binomials using a systematic method (grid or FOIL)
Collect like terms after expansion to simplify the result
Expand products involving negative terms correctly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} multiply out two brackets like (x + 3)(x − 2) and collect the terms to get x² + x − 6?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Quadratic Graphs
topics.description: Recognise that quadratic functions produce curved (parabolic) graphs, distinguish them from linear graphs, and use plotted quadratic graphs to estimate values and find approximate solutions
evidence: Explain why x² produces a U-shaped curve rather than a straight line
Plot a simple quadratic such as y = x² − 4 from a table of values
Read approximate solutions from a quadratic graph (e.g., where y = 0)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} recognise that an equation like y = x² produces a curved graph rather than a straight line, and use a plotted curve to estimate values?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simultaneous Equations
topics.description: Understand that two linear equations can be solved simultaneously by finding the point where their graphs intersect, and interpret this graphically and algebraically as the pair of values satisfying both equations
evidence: Explain that the intersection of two lines represents values satisfying both equations
Find the approximate solution to a pair of simultaneous equations by reading a graph
Verify a proposed solution by substituting into both equations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that solving two equations simultaneously means finding the one pair of values that satisfies both at once — and show what that looks like on a graph?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing groups: more or fewer
topics.description: Compare two groups of objects to determine which has more, fewer, or whether they are equal, using matching and counting strategies
evidence: Use one-to-one matching to compare two groups
State which group has more/fewer after counting both
Use the language 'equal to', 'more than', 'less than', 'fewer', 'most', 'least'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you put 6 raisins in one hand and 4 in the other and ask {{name}} which hand has more, can they work it out — either by counting or just by looking?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: How Many in Total?
topics.description: Cardinality principle: the last number said when counting a set tells how many objects are in the set, regardless of arrangement or order counted
evidence: After counting a set, answer 'how many?' with the last number stated
Understand that rearranging objects does not change the count
Understand that counting in a different order gives the same total
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} counts out 7 toy cars and you ask "so how many cars are there?", do they say "7" straight away — or do they count them all again from the start?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: One More Each Time
topics.description: Each successive counting number represents a quantity that is one larger than the previous number
evidence: Given a set of 5, know that adding one object makes 6
Explain that 8 is one more than 7
Given a number, identify one more and one less
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 5 stickers and you give them one more, do they know immediately there are now 6 — without needing to count all of them again from one?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: One-to-one counting
topics.description: One-to-one correspondence when counting objects: each object is paired with exactly one number name
evidence: Point to or touch each object exactly once while saying number names
Do not skip objects or double-count when counting a set
Recognise an error when someone counts an object twice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is counting a pile of grapes, do they touch or point to each one exactly once as they say each number — without skipping any or counting the same one twice?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Representing numbers with objects
topics.description: Represent numbers using objects, pictorial representations, and the number line
evidence: Show a given number using counters, cubes, or fingers
Draw a pictorial representation of a quantity (e.g. tally marks, dots)
Locate a number on a number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to show you what the number 5 looks like, can they do it in more than one way — such as drawing five dots, holding up five fingers, or pointing to 5 on a number line?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting in 2s
topics.description: Count in multiples of 2, 5, and 10 (skip counting)
evidence: Count 2, 4, 6, 8 … up to at least 20
Count 5, 10, 15, 20 … up to at least 50
Count 10, 20, 30 … up to 100
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is counting socks being paired up, can they skip-count in twos — 2, 4, 6, 8 — all the way to 20? Can they also count up in fives when counting coins, or in tens on a number line?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting objects to 20
topics.description: Count a set of objects to answer 'how many?' for sets up to 20 (arranged in lines, arrays, circles, or scattered)
evidence: Accurately count up to 20 objects in a line
Count up to 10 scattered objects without losing track
Given a number 1–20, count out that many objects from a larger set
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you spread out 15 buttons on the table in a random arrangement and ask {{name}} how many there are, can they count them all carefully and give you the right answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rote counting to 100
topics.description: Rote count forwards and backwards from 0 to 100, beginning from 0, 1, or any given number, by ones
evidence: Recite the number sequence 1–100 without skipping or repeating
Count backward from 20 to 0
Count forward starting from a number other than 1 (e.g. 'start at 23')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count out loud all the way from 0 to 100 — and if you say "start from 47", can they carry on from there without going back to the beginning?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two written numerals between 1 and 10
topics.description: Compare two written numerals between 1 and 10 to determine which is greater or less
evidence: Given two written numerals (e.g. 4 and 7), identify which is greater
Correctly use > and < or 'greater than' / 'less than' to compare single-digit numerals
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you write "3" and "8" on two pieces of paper and ask {{name}} which number is bigger, can they get it right — and could they tell you why?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in steps of 3 from 0
evidence: Count 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 … up to at least 30
Count backwards in 3s from 30
Identify the next number in a sequence of multiples of 3
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count in threes — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 — far enough to reach 30 without losing track or needing to start over?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards (age 6+)
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in tens from any number (not just multiples of 10)
evidence: Count 7, 17, 27, 37 … from a non-multiple starting point
Count backwards in tens from 83
Explain the pattern of adding/subtracting 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts at 37 and you ask them to count up in tens, can they say 37, 47, 57, 67 — crossing over into the next hundred without getting stuck?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting Within 1,000
topics.description: Count within 1000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s
evidence: Count forwards and backwards within 1000 from any starting number
Skip-count by 5s from any multiple of 5 to 1000
Skip-count by 100s from any number (e.g. 150, 250, 350 …)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count confidently up to 1000 — and if you ask them to count by hundreds from 200, or by tens from 650, can they do it without losing their place?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Skip Counting (4s, 8s, 50s, 100s)
topics.description: Count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50, and 100
evidence: Recite the multiples of 4 from 0 to at least 48
Recite the multiples of 8 from 0 to at least 96
Count in steps of 50 and 100 from 0 to 1000
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count in fours all the way to 48, count in eights, or count up in hundreds from any starting point — for example 350, 450, 550?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting in 6s
topics.description: Count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25, and 1000
evidence: Recite the multiples of 6 from 0 to at least 72
Recite the multiples of 7 from 0 to at least 84
Count in steps of 25 from 0 to 1000 and in steps of 1000 up to 10,000
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count in sevens — 7, 14, 21, 28 — or in nines, or in 25s when thinking about coins, or in 1000s when talking about distances like kilometres?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting into categories
topics.description: Classify objects into given categories, count the number in each category, and sort the categories by count
evidence: Sort a set of shapes by colour and count how many in each group
Sort objects by size (big/small) and state how many in each category
Identify which category has the most/fewest after sorting and counting
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} sort a pile of objects — like buttons, coins, or toy animals — into groups and count how many are in each group?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts
topics.description: Interpret and construct simple pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams, and simple tables
evidence: Read a pictogram where each symbol represents one item
Construct a tally chart from collected data
Draw a block diagram to represent data from a survey
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a simple chart or pictogram — like one showing how many children chose each favourite fruit — and answer questions like "which was most popular"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts (age 6+)
topics.description: Read, write, and use the vocabulary of data collection and display — data, tally, tally chart, frequency, frequency table, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete data, continuous data, line graph, pie chart — and apply these terms when collecting, organising, and presenting data
evidence: Correctly label the axes of a bar chart including a title, axis labels, and scale
Distinguish between discrete data (counted) and continuous data (measured) with an example of each
Use 'tally', 'frequency', and 'pictogram' correctly when describing how to record and display data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to show you how many books different children in their class read last month, could they draw a bar chart, label the axes, and explain what each bar represents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting Data into Categories
topics.description: Organise and represent data with up to three categories by counting objects in each category and sorting categories by quantity
evidence: Sort a set of objects into 2-3 given categories and count each group
Create a simple table or list showing category names and counts
Order categories from most to fewest or fewest to most
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at a collection of objects — like different coloured counters — sort them into up to three groups, count each group, and organise the results into a simple chart?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting into categories (age 6+)
topics.description: Interpret categorical data by asking and answering questions about totals, how many in each category, and how many more or less one category has than another
evidence: Answer 'how many?' for each category in a data set
Calculate the total number of data points across all categories
Compare two categories using 'how many more/fewer' language
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a chart showing how many children chose each flavour of ice cream, can they answer questions like "how many chose chocolate?" and "how many more chose vanilla than strawberry?"

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Picture & Bar Graphs
topics.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories; solve put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph
evidence: Draw a picture graph with a symbol representing one unit for each data point
Draw a bar graph with labelled axes and a single-unit scale
Use a bar graph to answer comparison questions (e.g. 'How many more votes did cats get than dogs?')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw a simple bar chart or picture graph to show information — like how many of each colour of sweet are in a bag — and answer questions from it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Bar graphs
topics.description: Interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs
evidence: Read a time graph showing temperature changes over a day
Present data about plant growth over weeks as a time graph
Explain the difference between a bar chart (discrete) and a time graph (continuous)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} choose the right type of chart for some data — for example, a bar chart for favourite colours or a line graph for temperature over a week — and draw it correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Representing numbers with objects (age 8+)
topics.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set; solve one- and two-step comparison, sum, and difference problems using bar charts, pictograms, and tables
evidence: Draw a bar graph where each square represents 5 pets
From a scaled pictogram, answer: how many more children chose football than tennis?
Solve a two-step problem: how many votes in total for the top two choices?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a bar chart showing how many books different children read last month, could they work out the total, find the difference between the most and least, and draw their own chart with a scale like "each square = 2 books"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and Comparing Bar Graphs
topics.description: Solve comparison, sum, and difference problems using information presented in a bar graph
evidence: Read a line graph of temperature over a week and identify the warmest day
Find the difference in rainfall between two months from a line graph
Explain what a rising/falling line means on a time-series graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a line graph showing how a plant's height changed over several weeks, can they read off values, spot when it grew fastest, and find the difference between two points?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading tables
topics.description: Complete, read, and interpret information in tables, including timetables
evidence: Read a bus timetable to find the departure time for a particular stop
Complete a two-way table from given data about favourite sports by gender
Calculate how long a train journey takes using a timetable
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a timetable — like a train or bus timetable — to find out when a journey leaves, arrives, and how long it takes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Statistical Analysis Vocabulary
topics.description: Read, write, and use the vocabulary of statistical analysis — mean, median, mode, range, frequency, data, sample, average, chart, table, graph, pie chart, scatter graph, correlation — with understanding of what each term describes
evidence: Correctly define and calculate the mean, median, mode, and range of a small data set
Use 'outlier' correctly to identify a value that doesn't fit the pattern, and explain its effect on the mean
Use 'correlation' correctly when describing the relationship shown in a scatter graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a set of test scores from their class, could they find the mean, the median, and the range — and explain what each one tells you about how the class did?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating the Mean
topics.description: Calculate and interpret the mean as an average of a data set
evidence: Calculate the mean of five test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95
Explain what the mean represents and how it differs from individual data values
Find a missing data value given the mean and all other values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the family scored 6, 8, 7, 5, and 9 on a board game over five rounds, can {{name}} work out the mean (average) score?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line graphs (age 10+)
topics.description: Interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs; use these to solve problems
evidence: Read values from a line graph showing temperature over a day and identify trends
Construct a pie chart from given data by calculating sector angles
Use a pie chart to determine the actual quantity represented by each sector given the total
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a pie chart — for example, one showing how a family spends its weekly budget — and use it to answer questions and solve problems?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); use operations on fractions to solve problems involving data in line plots (e.g. redistribute total equally)
evidence: Create a line plot showing lengths measured to the nearest 1/8 inch
Use the line plot to find the total of all measurements by adding fractions
Solve: 'If the total liquid were redistributed equally among all beakers, how much would each have?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the lengths of several objects to the nearest quarter or eighth of an inch and plotted them on a number line, could they use those measurements to work out totals or share amounts equally?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing measurements
topics.description: Describe, interpret, and compare distributions of a single variable using appropriate measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and spread (range), including the effect of outliers
evidence: Calculate mean, median, and mode for a data set and explain when each is most appropriate
Find the range of a data set and explain how an outlier affects the mean versus the median
Compare two data sets using their averages and ranges to draw conclusions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had the test scores of a whole class, could they find the mean, median, and range, and explain what each tells you about how the class performed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts (age 11+)
topics.description: Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, and vertical line charts for both categorical and grouped numerical data, choosing appropriate representations for the data type
evidence: Construct a grouped frequency table from raw continuous data, choosing appropriate class intervals
Draw a pie chart by calculating the angle for each category
Interpret a bar chart comparing two data sets and draw a conclusion about the difference
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} collects data for a project, can they choose the right type of chart to display it — and draw it accurately with correct labels and a suitable scale?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Scatter Graphs
topics.description: Plot bivariate data on a scatter graph with correctly labelled axes and appropriate scales; describe the correlation (positive, negative, none) and draw an estimated line of best fit where appropriate
evidence: Plot 10 data points on a scatter graph with correct axis labels and a consistent scale
Draw a line of best fit by eye, ensuring roughly equal numbers of points above and below
Use the line of best fit to estimate a y-value for a given x-value within the data range
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has data comparing hours of sleep and test scores for 10 students, can they plot the points on a scatter graph, draw a line of best fit, and use it to predict a score for someone who slept 7 hours?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Scatter Graphs & Correlation
topics.description: Describe simple mathematical relationships between two variables using scatter graphs, identify positive, negative, or no correlation, and use a line of best fit to make predictions
evidence: Plot bivariate data on a scatter graph and describe the type of correlation observed
Draw a line of best fit by eye and use it to estimate a value within the data range
Explain what positive, negative, and no correlation mean in the context of real data (e.g., temperature vs. ice-cream sales)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} plotted a scatter graph — say, comparing hours of revision and test scores — could they draw a line of best fit, describe the pattern, and use it to make a prediction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding halves and quarters (age 5+)
topics.description: Recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into four equal parts and identify each as 'a quarter'
Find a quarter of 12 objects by sharing into 4 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into quarters (four equal parts)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you fold a square piece of paper into four equal parts, can {{name}} tell you that each part is a quarter — and point to just one quarter?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Is a Half?
topics.description: Recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into two equal parts and identify each as 'a half'
Find half of 8 objects by sharing into 2 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into halves or not (equal vs unequal parts)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is helping share a sandwich equally between two people, can they cut it so both pieces are the same size — and tell you each piece is called a half?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decomposing a shape into more equal shares
topics.description: Understand that decomposing a shape into more equal shares creates smaller shares
evidence: Explain that a quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza
Demonstrate that fourths are smaller pieces than halves
Compare the size of halves and quarters of the same shape
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a pizza is shared between 2 people and then the same pizza is shared between 8 people, can {{name}} explain why each slice is smaller when more people share it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction Notation
topics.description: Read, write, and use fraction notation correctly — fraction, numerator, denominator, unit fraction, non-unit fraction, proper fraction, improper fraction, mixed number, equivalent fraction, simplest form — and understand what each term describes, including the roles of the numerator and denominator in expressing parts of a whole
evidence: Point to and name the numerator and denominator in any given fraction and explain what each tells you
Correctly classify fractions as unit, proper, improper, or mixed number with an example of each
Explain in own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent fractions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw the fraction 3/4 written down, could they point to the numerator and the denominator — and explain what each number actually means?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of amounts
topics.description: Recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
evidence: Find 1/3 of 12 objects by sharing into 3 equal groups
Shade 3/4 of a rectangle that has been divided into 4 equal parts
Identify 1/4 of a length on a number line or ruler
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you put 12 grapes on the table, can {{name}} count out a quarter of them — and then show you what three-quarters of the grapes looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves & Quarters of Shapes
topics.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares and describe them using the words halves, fourths, and quarters
evidence: Divide a circle into two equal halves
Divide a rectangle into four equal quarters
Describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a round pizza or a rectangular chocolate bar, can they divide it into four equal pieces and tell you each piece is called a quarter or a fourth?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
evidence: Write 1/2 of 10 = 5
Explain that 2/4 is the same as 1/2 using a diagram
Calculate simple unit fractions of quantities and write the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and eats half of them, can they write that as "1/2 of 6 = 3" — and explain why 2/4 and 1/2 are the same amount?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions
topics.description: Compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominator
evidence: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest
Explain that a larger denominator means smaller unit fractions
Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and explain that 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has eaten 3/8 of a cake and a friend has eaten 5/8 of the same cake, can they tell you who has eaten more — and put those fractions in order from smallest to biggest?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 7+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving counting in tenths, fractions of quantities, equivalence, fraction addition/subtraction, and fraction comparison
evidence: Solve a word problem requiring finding a fraction of a quantity
Solve a problem that requires comparing or ordering fractions
Choose and apply appropriate fraction knowledge to a multi-step problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bag of 20 sweets is shared equally among 5 friends, can {{name}} work out what fraction each person gets — and how many sweets that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions
topics.description: Recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators
evidence: Show that 1/2 = 2/4 using a diagram of equal parts
Use a fraction wall or bar model to find equivalent fractions
Explain why two fractions are equivalent by comparing the shaded areas
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a bar divided into 4 equal parts with 2 shaded, can they tell you that's the same as 1/2 — and draw a different bar showing the same amount another way?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line
topics.description: Recognise and use fractions as numbers: place unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators on a number line
evidence: Place 1/2, 1/4, 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1
Identify that 1/3 lies between 0 and 1/2 on the number line
Understand that a fraction is a single number, not just 'part of a shape'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you draw a number line from 0 to 1, can {{name}} mark where 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 should go — without any extra help?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple Fraction Sums
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7)
evidence: Calculate 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5
Calculate 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8
Explain that when denominators are the same, you add/subtract the numerators
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 2/8 of a cup of milk and then another 3/8 of a cup, can {{name}} work out the total without a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Splitting shapes into equal parts (age 7+)
topics.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares; describe shares as halves, thirds, and fourths; recognise that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape
evidence: Partition a circle into 3 equal parts and label each 'a third'
Partition a rectangle into 4 equal shares in more than one way
Explain that two different-looking shares can still be equal in size
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you cut a rectangle into thirds in two different ways (three strips vs three squares), can {{name}} recognise that both give equal thirds — even though the pieces look different?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths
topics.description: Count up and down in tenths; recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into 10 equal parts and from dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10
evidence: Count: one tenth, two tenths, three tenths … up to ten tenths (one whole)
Show that dividing a shape into 10 equal parts gives tenths
Explain that 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} splits a chocolate bar with 10 equal pieces, can they tell you each piece is one tenth — and count up from 1/10 to 10/10 in order?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unit fractions
topics.description: Recognise, find, and write fractions of a discrete set of objects: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators
evidence: Find 1/4 of 12 objects by dividing into 4 equal groups
Find 3/4 of 12 objects
Write the fraction of a set that is shaded or selected
topics.assessmentPrompt: If there are 15 books on a shelf, can {{name}} work out how many two-thirds of them is — and check by grouping the books into three equal piles?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, including results greater than one whole (e.g. 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8)
evidence: Calculate 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 and explain it equals 1 2/5
Subtract 2/6 from 5/6
Solve addition problems where the sum exceeds the whole: 7/8 + 3/8
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 5/8 of a bag of flour and then another 6/8, can {{name}} work out the total and explain what the answer means as a mixed number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 8+)
topics.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about size; record comparisons with >, =, or < symbols
evidence: Compare 3/8 and 3/4: same numerator, larger denominator means smaller pieces so 3/8 < 3/4
Compare 5/6 and 2/6: same denominator so 5/6 > 2/6
Justify a comparison using a visual model and explain why both fractions must refer to the same whole
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 3/5 and 3/8, can they tell you which is bigger just by thinking about the size of each piece — without needing to draw it out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal equivalents of tenths and hundredths
topics.description: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of any number of tenths or hundredths (e.g. 3/10 = 0.3, 27/100 = 0.27)
evidence: Write 7/10 as 0.7 and vice versa
Convert 45/100 to 0.45
Place 0.3 and 3/10 at the same point on a number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 7/10 on a price label, can they rewrite it as a decimal — and do the same thing for 43/100?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal & Percent Notation
topics.description: Read, write, and use decimal and percentage notation correctly — decimal, decimal point, tenths, hundredths, thousandths, percentage, per cent, % symbol, convert, terminating decimal — and understand the relationships between fractions, decimals, and percentages as three ways of expressing the same value
evidence: Read and write decimal numbers correctly, identifying the value of each digit (ones, tenths, hundredths)
Use the % symbol correctly and explain that per cent means 'out of 100'
Convert between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages (e.g. 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) and explain why they are equal
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw '0.5' and '50%' written down, could they explain that they both mean the same amount — and write them as a fraction too?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value
topics.description: Round decimals with one decimal place to the nearest whole number
evidence: Round 3.7 to 4 and 3.2 to 3
Place 6.5 on a number line between 6 and 7 and decide it rounds to 7
Round a set of one-decimal-place numbers and explain the rounding rule
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures something as 3.7 m, can they tell you whether that rounds to 3 m or 4 m — and explain why?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value (age 8+)
topics.description: Compare numbers with the same number of decimal places up to two decimal places
evidence: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest
Compare 3.72 and 3.27 using place-value reasoning
Place three two-decimal-place numbers on a number line in order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing two prices — £4.75 and £4.57 — can they tell you which is more expensive without using a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals and fractions
topics.description: Solve simple measure and money problems involving fractions and decimals to two decimal places
evidence: Calculate 1/4 of £3.20
A rope is 2.5 m long; how much is left after cutting 0.75 m?
Find 3/10 of 1 kg and express the answer in grams and as a decimal of a kg
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bottle holds 1.5 litres and {{name}} drinks 0.75 litres, can they work out how much is left — and write it as both a decimal and a fraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing by 10 and 100
topics.description: Find the effect of dividing a one- or two-digit number by 10 and 100, identifying the value of the digits as ones, tenths, and hundredths
evidence: Calculate 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 and identify 3 as ones and 7 as tenths
Calculate 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 and identify 4 as hundredths
Explain that dividing by 10 shifts each digit one place to the right
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts with the number 48 and divides it by 10, can they tell you the answer — and explain what happened to each digit's place value?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions (age 8+)
topics.description: Generate simple equivalent fractions and explain why they are equivalent using visual fraction models
evidence: Given 1/3, generate 2/6 as equivalent and show with area model
Simplify 4/8 to 1/2 and justify with a fraction strip
Complete equivalence chains: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a fraction bar split into 3 parts with 1 shaded (= 1/3), can they draw an equivalent bar with 6 parts that shows exactly the same amount shaded?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions on a number line
topics.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent if they are the same size or the same point on a number line; recognise and show families of common equivalent fractions using diagrams
evidence: Use fraction strips to show 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6
Verify on a number line that 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point
Identify at least three fractions equivalent to 1/2 using diagrams
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that 2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same point on a number line, can they explain in their own words why those two fractions are equal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction-Decimal Equivalents
