topics.description: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4
evidence: Match fractions to decimals in a sorting activity
Explain why 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 using a hundredths grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 3/4 of a cup of flour, can {{name}} tell you what that is as a decimal — without looking it up?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions as parts of shapes
topics.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole
evidence: Partition a rectangle into 6 equal-area parts and label each 1/6
Show two different ways to partition a square into 4 equal parts
Given a pre-partitioned shape, write the unit fraction for one part
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to fold a square piece of paper into 8 equal parts, can they tell you what fraction of the whole square each part represents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of amounts (harder)
topics.description: Solve problems involving increasingly harder fractions to calculate quantities, including non-unit fractions where the answer is a whole number
evidence: Find 3/5 of 20
Calculate 2/3 of 18 and explain the two-step process (divide then multiply)
Solve: A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red — how many red sweets?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If 3/4 of a class of 28 pupils brought their homework in, can {{name}} work out exactly how many pupils that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole
topics.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a/b as a parts of size 1/b
evidence: Given a shape divided into 5 equal parts, identify one shaded part as 1/5
Explain that 3/4 means 3 parts each of size 1/4
Draw a model showing 2/6 as 2 pieces of a whole cut into 6
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you cut a pizza into 6 equal slices, can {{name}} explain what 1/6 means — and then work out what 4/6 of the pizza looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole (age 8+)
topics.description: Express whole numbers as fractions (e.g. 3 = 3/1) and recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers (e.g. 4/4 = 1, 6/1 = 6)
evidence: Write 5 as 5/1 and explain why
Locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point on a number line
Identify which fractions from a list equal a whole number: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to write the number 3 as a fraction, can they write 3/1 — and also tell you what fraction equals exactly 1 whole, like 4/4 or 5/5?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line (age 8+)
topics.description: Represent fractions on a number line: partition the interval 0 to 1 into b equal parts to locate 1/b, then mark off a lengths of 1/b from 0 to locate a/b
evidence: Partition a 0-to-1 number line into 4 equal parts and mark 1/4
Explain that each part on the line has size 1/b
Locate 1/3 and 1/6 on separate number lines
Locate 3/4 on a number line by counting three 1/4-jumps from 0
Place 5/6 on a number line and explain the process
Identify a fraction shown by a point on a pre-partitioned number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a number line from 0 to 1 split into 5 equal parts, can they label where 2/5 and 4/5 go — and explain how they worked it out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths (age 8+)
topics.description: Count up and down in hundredths; recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by 100 or dividing tenths by 10
evidence: Count from 3/100 to 12/100 in hundredths
Explain that 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100
Place several hundredths on a number line between 0 and 1/10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has £1 and spends 37p, can they say that 37p is 37/100 of a pound — and count up in hundredths from 0/100 to 100/100?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers
topics.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, including by converting to improper fractions or using properties of operations
evidence: Calculate 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 and express as a mixed number
Subtract 3 1/4 from 5 3/4
Solve 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 by regrouping the whole number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 1 and 2/5 cups of oats and another batch needs 2 and 3/5 cups, can {{name}} add them together to get the total — including converting when the fifths add up past a whole?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding fractions (different denominators)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with denominators that are multiples of the same number by finding a common denominator
evidence: Calculate 1/3 + 1/6 by converting to sixths: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2
Calculate 3/4 − 1/8 by converting to eighths
Add 2/5 + 3/10 and simplify the answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 1/3 and 1/6, can they find a common denominator and work out the total — showing their working?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with like denominators, using visual models and equations
evidence: A jug contains 3/4 litre of juice; 2/4 litre is poured out — how much remains?
Two pieces of ribbon are 2 3/8 and 1 5/8 inches — what is their total length?
Draw a fraction model to represent and solve a fraction word problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that one section of a nature trail is 3/8 km and another is 5/8 km, can they work out the total distance without a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Decimals
topics.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths (or up to three decimal places) by reasoning about size using place-value understanding; record with >, =, <
evidence: Compare 0.45 and 0.405 and explain which is greater
Order 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 from smallest to largest
Justify that 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 using place-value reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares 0.45 and 0.54, can they use place value to explain which is bigger — without reaching for a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 9+)
topics.description: Compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators by creating common denominators/numerators or comparing to a benchmark such as 1/2; justify conclusions with visual models
evidence: Compare 3/8 and 5/12 by finding a common denominator of 24
Order 2/3, 3/5, and 7/10 from smallest to largest
Use the benchmark 1/2 to decide that 5/8 > 3/7
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has eaten 2/3 of their lunch and a friend has eaten 3/4 of theirs, can they work out who's eaten more — by finding a common way to compare the fractions?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Converting tenths to hundredths
topics.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100 and use this to add fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (e.g. 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100)
evidence: Rewrite 7/10 as 70/100
Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 using a hundredths grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 3/10 and 17/100, can they rewrite 3/10 as hundredths first — and then add the two fractions together?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value (age 9+)
topics.description: Round decimals with two decimal places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place
evidence: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (3) and to 1 d.p. (3.5)
Round 12.95 to 1 d.p. (13.0) and explain the boundary case
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures a length as 4.67 m, can they round it to the nearest whole metre — and also to the nearest tenth of a metre?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals for Tenths & Hundredths
topics.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100; read and write decimal numbers as fractions (e.g. 0.62 = 62/100, 0.71 = 71/100)
evidence: Rewrite 0.62 as 62/100
Write 3/10 as 0.3 and locate on a number line
Read 0.07 and express as 7/100
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a price tag showing £0.65, can they rewrite it as a fraction — and go the other way, turning 47/100 into a decimal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals to three places
topics.description: Solve problems involving numbers with up to three decimal places
evidence: Calculate the total of three measurements: 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m
A bottle holds 1.5 litres; 0.375 l is poured out — how much remains?
Find two numbers with 3 d.p. that add to make 1
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling a tank that holds 5.000 litres and has poured in 2.375 litres, can they work out how much more is needed to fill it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions (age 9+)
topics.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to (n×a)/(n×b) using visual models; use this principle to recognise and generate equivalent fractions, including tenths and hundredths
evidence: Use a fraction strip to show 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9
Explain that multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction because the size of the whole is unchanged
Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify with diagrams
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make 2/3 look different without changing its value, can they multiply the top and bottom by the same number and explain why the fraction stays the same?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction Addition Concepts
topics.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts; decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way
evidence: Write two different decompositions of 5/6
Use a visual model to justify a decomposition of 2 1/8 into whole-number and fraction parts
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 7/8 of a chocolate bar and gives away 3/8, can they work out what fraction is left — and then show two different ways to split 7/8 into two parts?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual models and equations
evidence: Each person eats 3/8 of a pizza and there are 5 people — how many pizzas are needed?
A ribbon is cut into pieces of 2/3 metre; how long are 4 pieces altogether?
Between what two whole numbers does 6 × 3/4 lie?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If each section of a garden uses 3/4 of a bag of compost and there are 4 sections, can {{name}} work out how many bags are needed in total?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mixed numbers and improper fractions
topics.description: Recognise mixed numbers and improper fractions; convert from one form to the other (e.g. 2/5 + 4/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5)
evidence: Convert 11/4 to 2 3/4
Convert 3 2/5 to 17/5
Write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 = 2 as both improper fraction and whole number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the fraction 9/4, can they convert it to a mixed number — and then turn 2 and 3/5 back into an improper fraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying fractions
topics.description: Understand a/b as a multiple of 1/b; multiply proper fractions and mixed numbers by whole numbers, supported by visual models (e.g. 3 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5)
evidence: Calculate 4 × 3/8 using repeated addition or the rule n × a/b = (n×a)/b
Multiply 2 1/3 × 3 and express as a mixed number
Use a visual model to show why 5 × 1/4 = 5/4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a cup of butter and {{name}} wants to make it three times over, can they work out how much butter they need in total?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Percentage and decimal equivalents
topics.description: Solve problems requiring knowledge of percentage and decimal equivalents of 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and fractions with denominators that are multiples of 10 or 25
evidence: State that 1/5 = 20% = 0.2 and use this to find 20% of 60
Convert 3/4 to 75% and to 0.75
A shop offers 25% off a £40 item — what is the sale price?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that 1/4 = 25% = 0.25, can they use that to work out 25% of £80 — and also find 4/5 of 60 sweets?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths (age 9+)
topics.description: Recognise and use thousandths; relate them to tenths, hundredths, and their decimal equivalents (e.g. 1/1000 = 0.001, 35/1000 = 0.035)
evidence: Explain that 1 tenth = 100 thousandths
Place 0.345 on a number line between 0.34 and 0.35
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the decimal 0.003, can they write it as a fraction and tell you roughly where it sits on a number line between 0 and 0.01?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions (age 9+)
topics.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b (e.g. 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5)
evidence: Express 5/8 as a sum of five copies of 1/8
Show on a number line how 4/3 is built by iterating 1/3 four times
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to show 4/5 as a sum of smaller equal fractions, can they write it out as 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding Percentages
topics.description: Understand the per cent symbol (%); know that per cent means ‘number of parts per hundred’; write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal
evidence: Write 35% as 35/100 and as 0.35
Shade 40% of a 10×10 grid and write the fraction 40/100
Explain that 100% means the whole, 50% means half
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a shop advertises 50% off, can {{name}} explain that this means half price — and write 50% as both a fraction and a decimal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Fractions (Unlike Denominators)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator
evidence: Compute 2/3 + 5/4 by converting to twelfths: 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12
Subtract 1 3/5 from 3 1/4 using a common denominator
Explain the strategy of finding a common denominator and verify using a visual model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a cup of one ingredient and 3/4 of another, can {{name}} add those fractions together — even though the denominators are different?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area with Fractions
topics.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit-fraction squares; show that the area equals the product of the side lengths
evidence: Tile a 2/3 × 3/4 rectangle with 1/12 squares and count to find area = 6/12 = 1/2
Explain why the number of unit-fraction tiles equals the product of the two fractions
Calculate the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 using fraction multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a piece of fabric is 2/3 m long and 3/4 m wide, can {{name}} work out its area — and explain how tiling it with tiny fraction-squares shows the same answer as multiplying?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 10+)
topics.description: Compare and order fractions including fractions greater than 1, by converting to common denominators or using benchmarks
evidence: Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, and 11/12 from smallest to largest
Compare 7/5 and 4/3 using common denominators
Place improper fractions and mixed numbers on a number line in correct order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to sort 5/3, 7/4, and 2/1 in order from smallest to biggest, can they convert them to a common denominator and order them correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals and fractions (age 10+)
topics.description: Associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents for simple fractions (e.g. 3/8 = 0.375); recall and use equivalences between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages in different contexts
evidence: Convert 3/8 to 0.375 by dividing 3 ÷ 8
State that 1/5 = 0.2 = 20% from memory
Use fraction–decimal–percentage equivalences to compare 30%, 1/3, and 0.35 and put them in order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 3/8 written on a worksheet, can they convert it to a decimal — and also say roughly what percentage that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing by Fractions
topics.description: Interpret and compute division of a whole number by a unit fraction (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain why the quotient is larger than the dividend
evidence: Compute 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 and explain: 'How many fifths fit in 4 wholes?'
Create a story context for 6 ÷ (1/4) and solve it
Verify 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 by showing 20 × (1/5) = 4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you have 4 metres of ribbon and each bow needs 1/5 of a metre, can {{name}} work out how many bows you can make — and explain why the answer is bigger than 4?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing fractions (unit fractions)
topics.description: Interpret and compute division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain the result
evidence: Compute (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 and explain using a visual model of splitting 1/3 into 4 equal parts
Create a story context for (1/6) ÷ 3 and solve it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 1/3 of a bag of rice and splits it into 4 equal portions, can they work out what fraction of the whole bag each portion is — and explain why the answer is smaller than 1/3?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing unit fractions and whole numbers
topics.description: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions, using visual models and equations
evidence: Solve: '3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally — how much each?' (1/6 lb)
Solve: 'How many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups of raisins?' (6 servings)
Create a story context for a given unit-fraction division expression
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has half a pizza to share equally among 3 people, can they work out what fraction of the whole pizza each person gets — and explain the steps they took?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole (age 10+)
topics.description: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b); solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to fractional or mixed-number answers
evidence: Explain that 3/4 means 3 ÷ 4 and verify by showing 3/4 × 4 = 3
Solve: '9 people share a 50-pound sack equally — how many pounds each?' and express the answer as 5 5/9
Use a visual model to show that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each person 3/4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shares 3 pizzas equally among 4 friends, can they work out what fraction each person gets — and explain why 3 ÷ 4 gives the same answer as 3/4?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction Word Problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with unlike denominators, using visual models and benchmark fractions to estimate and assess reasonableness
evidence: Solve: 'Tara ate 2/5 of a pizza and Sam ate 1/3. How much did they eat together?'
Recognise that 2/5 + 1/2 ≠ 3/7 because 3/7 < 1/2 but the sum should exceed 1/2
Estimate a fraction sum using benchmarks (0, 1/2, 1) before computing exactly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} walks 1 and 1/2 miles to school and 3/4 of a mile to a friend's house, can they work out the total distance — and check whether their answer makes sense?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication as scaling
topics.description: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to a factor based on the size of the other factor without computing; explain the effect of multiplying by fractions greater than, equal to, or less than 1
evidence: Predict without calculating whether 3/4 × 7 is greater or less than 7
Explain why multiplying by 5/3 makes a number larger and multiplying by 2/5 makes it smaller
Relate multiplying a/b by n/n = 1 to the principle of fraction equivalence
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} multiplies 20 by 1/4, can they predict whether the answer will be bigger or smaller than 20 — and explain why, before doing the calculation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying fractions (age 10+)
topics.description: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, including proper fractions by proper fractions; interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of q partitioned into b equal parts; write answers in simplest form
evidence: Compute (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15 and show with an area model
Use a visual model to demonstrate (2/3) × 4 = 8/3 = 2 2/3
Simplify the product 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a bag of flour and {{name}} only wants to make 3/4 of the recipe, can they multiply those fractions to find out how much flour they need?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Real-world fraction multiplication
topics.description: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, using visual fraction models or equations
evidence: Solve: 'A recipe needs 2 1/3 cups of flour; you want to make 1 1/2 batches. How much flour?'
Draw a fraction model to represent and solve a multiplication word problem
Check the reasonableness of a fraction product in context using estimation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe makes 12 biscuits using 1 and 1/2 cups of sugar, and {{name}} wants to make only 2/3 of the recipe, can they work out how much sugar they need?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simplifying Fractions
topics.description: Use common factors to simplify fractions to their simplest form; use common multiples to express fractions with a common denominator
evidence: Simplify 18/24 to 3/4 by identifying the HCF of 18 and 24
Express 2/3 and 5/8 with a common denominator of 24
Explain why dividing numerator and denominator by a common factor produces an equivalent fraction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has the fraction 12/16, can they simplify it to its lowest terms — and explain what they divided the top and bottom by?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals and fractions (age 11+)
topics.description: Work interchangeably with terminating decimals and their corresponding fractions (such as 3.5 and 7/2 or 0.375 and 3/8); convert fluently between the two forms
evidence: Convert any terminating decimal to a fraction in simplest form
Convert any fraction with a denominator whose prime factors are only 2 and 5 to a terminating decimal
Explain why some fractions produce terminating decimals and others do not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 0.375 on a calculator display, can they convert it to a fraction in its simplest form — without using the calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing fractions
topics.description: Divide a fraction by a fraction using the 'keep-change-flip' method and visual models; interpret and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions
evidence: Divide a fraction by a fraction using the reciprocal method
Use visual fraction models to represent and explain fraction division
Create story contexts for fraction division problems and solve them
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 3/4 of a litre of juice and each glass holds 3/8 of a litre, can they work out how many glasses they can fill — using fraction division?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mixed & Improper Fractions
topics.description: Use the four operations with formal written methods applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative
evidence: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide with positive and negative integers
Apply formal written methods to calculations with decimals of any size
Perform all four operations with proper fractions, improper fractions, and mixed numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out −1/2 + 3/4 − 1 and 1/4 as part of a longer problem, can they do it using written methods — showing each step clearly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying fractions (age 11+)
topics.description: Interpret fractions and percentages as operators — find a fraction or percentage of an amount by multiplying, understanding that 'of' means multiply (e.g., 3/4 of 200 = 3/4 × 200 = 150)
evidence: Calculate a fraction of a given amount by multiplying
Calculate a percentage of a given amount by converting to a decimal and multiplying
Use the operator interpretation to solve multi-step problems involving discounts, taxes, and portions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a £120 jacket is reduced by 35%, can {{name}} work out the sale price — by first calculating 35% of £120 and then subtracting?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 2-D shapes
topics.description: Recognise and name common 2-D shapes (circles, triangles, rectangles including squares)
evidence: Name a triangle, circle, rectangle, and square when shown them
Identify a shape correctly regardless of its size or orientation
Pick out all the triangles from a mixed set of shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} point to shapes around the house — like a clock, a window, or a pizza — and correctly name whether each is a circle, triangle, rectangle, or square?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 3-D shapes
topics.description: Recognise and name common 3-D shapes (cubes, cuboids, pyramids, spheres, cylinders, cones)
evidence: Name a cube, sphere, cylinder, and cone when shown them
Identify 3-D shapes in the environment (e.g. a tin is a cylinder)
Recognise a cuboid and a pyramid among a set of solid shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name common 3-D shapes they find around them — like a tin of beans (cylinder), a ball (sphere), or a dice (cube)?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Positional Language
topics.description: Describe the position of objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, next to
evidence: Describe a toy as being 'on top of' the table
Follow instructions like 'put the cube behind the box'
Use 'left' and 'right' in simple contexts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give directions to find something around the house using words like "above," "below," "beside," "in front of," or "behind"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 3-D shapes (age 5+)
topics.description: Analyse and compare 2-D and 3-D shapes using informal language to describe sides, vertices, and other attributes
evidence: Count the sides and corners of a shape
Compare a triangle and a rectangle by number of sides
Describe a cube as having 'square faces' and 'corners'
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe what makes two shapes different — for example, explaining that a triangle has 3 corners and 3 sides while a square has 4 of each?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Building & Drawing Shapes
topics.description: Model shapes by building from components (e.g. sticks and clay balls) and by drawing
evidence: Build a triangle from three sticks and three clay balls
Draw a recognisable rectangle
Construct a cube from straws and connectors
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} build or draw a shape they've been shown — for example, making a cube from folded paper or copying a triangle onto dot paper?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Combining Simple Shapes
topics.description: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes (e.g. two triangles make a rectangle)
evidence: Join two triangles to make a rectangle or larger triangle
Use pattern blocks to fill a hexagon outline
Create a picture or design by combining basic shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} fit smaller shapes together to make bigger ones — like combining two triangles to make a rectangle?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Flat vs Solid Shapes
topics.description: Distinguish two-dimensional (flat) shapes from three-dimensional (solid) shapes
evidence: Sort shapes into 'flat' and 'solid' groups
Explain that a circle is flat but a sphere is solid
Identify whether a given shape is 2-D or 3-D
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand the difference between a flat shape like a square and a solid shape like a cube — and can they sort everyday objects into flat or solid?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Turns & Directions
topics.description: Describe movement and direction, including whole, half, quarter, and three-quarter turns
evidence: Follow instructions to move forward, backward, turn left/right
Demonstrate a whole turn, half turn, and quarter turn with their body
Describe a route using directional language
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is playing a game where they have to turn left or right, do they understand what a quarter turn, half turn, and full turn mean?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 2-D faces on 3-D shapes
topics.description: Identify 2-D shapes on the surface of 3-D shapes (e.g. a circle on a cylinder, a triangle on a pyramid)
evidence: Point out a circular face on a cylinder or cone
Identify triangular faces on a pyramid
Recognise that the faces of 3-D shapes are 2-D shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at a 3-D shape and name the 2-D shapes on its faces — for example, saying a cylinder has circles on the ends and a rectangle wrapped round the side?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 2-D shapes (age 6+)
topics.description: Identify and describe properties of 2-D shapes including the number of sides and line symmetry in a vertical line
evidence: Count the number of sides of a given 2-D shape
Identify whether a 2-D shape has a vertical line of symmetry
Use properties (number of sides, symmetry) to describe and distinguish between shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count the sides of a shape and say whether it has a line of symmetry — for example, knowing that a rectangle is symmetrical but a scalene triangle is not?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angles in triangles (age 6+)
topics.description: Distinguish defining attributes of shapes (e.g. triangles are closed and three-sided) from non-defining attributes (e.g. colour, orientation, overall size)
evidence: Build and draw shapes that possess defining attributes
Identify that a shape remains a triangle regardless of its size, colour, or orientation
Explain why a given shape is or is not a particular type based on its defining properties
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that what makes a shape a triangle is having 3 sides and 3 corners — not its colour or which way it's pointing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Building with 3-D Shapes
topics.description: Compose three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, right circular cylinders) and create composite shapes; build new shapes from component shapes
evidence: Stack cubes and prisms to build towers or structures
Combine 3-D shapes to make a new solid (e.g. cone on top of cylinder)
Describe a composite 3-D shape in terms of its component shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} combine 3-D shapes — like stacking cubes and cylinders — to build a new composite solid?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Composing Shapes
topics.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, quarter-circles) to create composite shapes, and compose new shapes from the composite shape
evidence: Combine two triangles to form a rectangle or larger triangle
Put together half-circles and quarter-circles to form circles or new shapes
Decompose a composite shape and describe which simpler shapes make it up
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use flat shapes like triangles and rectangles to fit together and make a new larger shape — like a puzzle?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Edges, vertices, and faces
topics.description: Identify and describe properties of 3-D shapes including the number of edges, vertices, and faces
evidence: Count the edges, vertices, and faces of common 3-D shapes
Use the terms edge, vertex (vertices), and face correctly
Describe a 3-D shape by its properties (e.g. a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count the faces, edges, and vertices of a 3-D shape like a cube or triangular prism?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Patterns & Sequences
topics.description: Order and arrange combinations of mathematical objects in patterns and sequences
evidence: Continue a repeating pattern of shapes or colours
Describe the rule for a given sequence of objects
Create own patterns and sequences using mathematical objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} spot a repeating pattern made of shapes or objects and continue it, or create their own repeating pattern?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Position, direction, and movement
topics.description: Use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction, and movement, including straight lines and distinguishing rotation as a turn in terms of right angles (quarter, half, three-quarter turns, clockwise and anti-clockwise)
evidence: Use terms such as clockwise, anti-clockwise, quarter turn, half turn, three-quarter turn
Describe a right angle as a quarter turn
Give and follow directions involving straight-line movement and turns
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} follow directions like "turn clockwise a quarter turn" or "move three squares to the right" on a grid or in a simple navigation game?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting 2-D and 3-D shapes
topics.description: Compare and sort common 2-D and 3-D shapes and everyday objects by their properties
evidence: Sort a collection of 2-D shapes by number of sides
Sort 3-D shapes by number of faces or whether faces are flat/curved
Explain criteria used to sort a group of shapes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} sort a collection of shapes into groups — for example, separating all the shapes with curved sides from those with only straight sides?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 2-D shapes (age 7+)
topics.description: Draw 2-D shapes and make 3-D shapes using modelling materials; recognise 3-D shapes in different orientations and describe them
evidence: Draw a triangle, rectangle, pentagon, or hexagon accurately
Construct a cube or cuboid from modelling materials (e.g. straws and connectors)
Recognise a 3-D shape (e.g. a pyramid) when it is rotated or seen from a different angle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a cube to look at, can they draw it on paper — and then make a cube-shaped model from modelling clay or construction materials?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angles in triangles (age 7+)
topics.description: Recognise and draw shapes having specified attributes (e.g. a given number of angles or equal faces); identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes
evidence: Draw a shape with exactly 5 sides (pentagon)
Identify all quadrilaterals in a set of mixed shapes
Name and draw a hexagon, explaining it has 6 sides and 6 angles
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given instructions like "draw a shape with 5 sides" or "draw a shape with all equal angles," can they draw it correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Parallel and perpendicular lines
topics.description: Identify horizontal and vertical lines and pairs of perpendicular and parallel lines
evidence: Point out horizontal and vertical lines in shapes and real-world contexts
Identify a pair of parallel lines (lines that never meet and are always the same distance apart)
Identify perpendicular lines (lines that meet at a right angle)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a set of railway tracks or a window frame, can they point to which lines are parallel (never crossing) and which are perpendicular (meeting at a right angle)?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Right Angles & Turns
topics.description: Identify right angles; recognise that two right angles make a half-turn, three make three-quarters, and four make a complete turn
evidence: Use a right-angle checker to identify right angles in shapes and the environment
Classify angles as right angles, less than a right angle, or greater than a right angle
Explain that 4 right angles make a full turn (360°)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the corner of a piece of paper, can they tell you that's a right angle — and that spinning all the way round takes four right angles?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding angles
topics.description: Recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn
evidence: Identify angles at the corners of 2-D shapes
Describe a turn (e.g. quarter turn, half turn) in terms of the angle made
Explain that an angle measures the amount of turn between two lines meeting at a point
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to point to an angle on the corner of a book or door frame, can they find it — and explain that swinging a door open is also a kind of turn (angle)?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 2-D shapes (age 8+)
topics.description: Identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations; recognise line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry
evidence: Find all lines of symmetry in a rectangle, square, and equilateral triangle
Determine whether a given shape has a line of symmetry when rotated
Identify which shapes in a set have exactly one line of symmetry
Determine how many lines of symmetry a regular hexagon has
Draw all lines of symmetry for a given figure
Identify which figures from a set are not line-symmetric
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a picture of a butterfly or a star shape, can they draw the line (or lines) where you could fold it exactly in half so both sides match?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Coordinates (age 8+)
topics.description: Plot specified points on a coordinate grid and draw sides to complete a given polygon
evidence: Plot points (1,1), (1,4), (5,4), (5,1) and join to make a rectangle
Given three vertices of a square, plot the fourth vertex
Complete a triangle by plotting the third vertex at given coordinates and drawing sides
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given three coordinate pairs on a grid, can they plot each point and then connect the dots to draw the correct triangle or rectangle?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Describing Movements
topics.description: Describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down
evidence: Describe moving from (2,3) to (5,3) as 3 units to the right
Translate a shape 4 units right and 2 units up and state the new coordinates
Predict where a point will be after a given translation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a shape is at position (2, 3) on a grid and you tell {{name}} to move it four squares right and two squares up, can they work out its new position without drawing it first?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: First Quadrant Coordinates
topics.description: Describe positions on a 2-D grid as coordinates in the first quadrant
evidence: Read the coordinates of a point on a grid as (3, 5)
Explain that the first number is the horizontal distance and the second is the vertical distance
Identify the coordinates of all vertices of a shape plotted on a grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is playing a grid-based treasure map game, can they correctly say where the treasure is using two numbers — like "three across and four up" — from the corner?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Lines of symmetry
topics.description: Complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry
evidence: Given half a butterfly shape and a mirror line, complete the other half on a grid
Complete a symmetric pattern on squared paper with a vertical line of symmetry
Check a completed figure by folding along the mirror line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} half a shape drawn on squared paper with a mirror line marked, can they draw the missing half so the whole shape is perfectly symmetrical?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Nets of 3-D Shapes
topics.description: Identify, draw, and interpret nets of common 3-D shapes — cubes, cuboids, triangular prisms, and square-based pyramids — by predicting which 3-D shape a given flat arrangement of faces will fold into, checking whether a net will close completely, and sketching a net from a description or 3-D model; understand the relationship between the number of faces and the structure of the net
evidence: Draw the net of a cube, cuboid, or triangular prism and fold it mentally to identify which faces connect
Build a 3-D shape from its net and check that all faces, edges, and vertices match
Identify which of several given nets will fold into a specific 3-D shape and explain why the others won't
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a flat T-shaped piece of card with six squares, can they tell you — before folding — that it makes a cube, and point out which square will become each face?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Transformations on a grid
topics.description: Represent and carry out geometric transformations on squared paper or a coordinate grid: reflections (in horizontal, vertical, and diagonal mirror lines, including the axes), translations (described as a vector or as left/right/up/down moves), and rotations (90° or 180° about a stated centre point); describe each transformation precisely using the correct language; identify which transformation maps one shape onto its image by comparing position, orientation, and size
evidence: Reflect a shape in a given mirror line on a grid and label the new coordinates
Translate a shape by a given number of squares horizontally and vertically and describe the movement
Rotate a shape 90° or 180° about a given centre on a grid and check the image is congruent to the original
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a shape and its mirror image on squared paper, can they draw in the exact mirror line, and describe the reflection precisely — including where the line of reflection is — without just saying 'it flipped'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Types of angles
topics.description: Identify acute and obtuse angles; compare and order angles up to two right angles by size
evidence: Classify given angles as acute, right, or obtuse
Order four angles from smallest to largest by visual comparison
Identify all acute and obtuse angles in a given triangle or quadrilateral
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the hands on a clock showing different times, can they tell you which angle between the hands is acute (sharper than a right angle) and which is obtuse (wider)?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Types of angles (age 8+)
topics.description: Use and interpret standard geometric diagram conventions: mark right angles with a small square, equal lengths with single or double tick marks, and equal angles with arc marks; label angles in three-letter notation (∠ABC) and individual angles with a single letter or number; draw diagrams showing angles at a point, angles on a straight line, and angles inside polygons with these conventions; read diagrams with these marks to identify given information and find unknown values
evidence: Mark a right angle with a small square symbol in a diagram and explain what it means
Use tick marks to show equal lengths in a shape and double tick marks for a second pair of equal sides
Read and interpret angle notation (e.g. angle ABC) and identify the angle being referred to in a diagram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s maths diagram shows a small square in one corner and matching arc marks on two other angles, can they tell you what each mark means — and use them to figure out a missing angle without re-measuring?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding angles (age 8+)
topics.description: Understand that shapes in different categories may share attributes defining a larger category; classify quadrilaterals (rhombuses, rectangles, squares) and draw examples of quadrilaterals not in those subcategories
evidence: Explain that a square is a special rectangle and also a special rhombus
Sort shapes into a Venn diagram: quadrilaterals vs rectangles vs squares
Draw a quadrilateral that is not a rectangle, rhombus, or square
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a square, a rectangle, and a rhombus, can they explain what makes them all quadrilaterals — and what makes each one different from the others?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 3-D shapes (age 9+)
topics.description: Identify 3-D shapes, including cubes and other cuboids, from 2-D representations
evidence: Identify a cuboid from its net
Name the 3-D shape shown in an isometric drawing
Match 2-D representations to the correct 3-D shape
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a flat architect's sketch of a box or a pyramid, can they tell you the name of the 3-D shape it represents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angle Sum Rules
topics.description: Know that angles at a point sum to 360° (one whole turn), angles on a straight line sum to 180°, and vertically opposite angles are equal; use these facts to find missing angles
evidence: State that two angles on a straight line add to 180°
Explain that four right angles at a point make 360°
Identify 270° as three right angles
topics.assessmentPrompt: If three angles meet at a point and two of them are 120° and 95°, can {{name}} work out the third angle — knowing all the angles at a point add up to 360°?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Classifying shapes by line properties
topics.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or angles of a specified size; recognise right triangles as a category
evidence: Sort a set of quadrilaterals into those with parallel sides and those without
Identify which triangles in a set are right triangles
Classify shapes that have both perpendicular and parallel sides
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a mixed set of triangles and quadrilaterals, can they sort them into groups — like "shapes with at least one right angle" or "shapes with parallel sides" — and explain their reasoning?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Degrees and turns
topics.description: Know that angles are measured in degrees, where one degree is 1/360 of a full turn; understand that an angle turning through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees
evidence: Explain that a full turn is 360° and a right angle is 90°
Describe what 'one degree' means in terms of a fraction of a circle
State that an angle of 45° has turned through 45 one-degree angles
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a full circle is 360 degrees, can they tell you how many degrees a quarter turn is — and explain roughly what one single degree looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating Angles
topics.description: Estimate and compare acute, obtuse, and reflex angles in degrees; classify angles by type and order them by size
evidence: Estimate an angle as approximately 130° and classify it as obtuse
Identify a reflex angle in a diagram and estimate it as about 270°
Order four angles from smallest to largest by estimation before measuring
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} three different angles drawn on paper, can they estimate which is biggest, label each as acute, obtuse, or reflex — and then check with a protractor?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Lines, Rays & Angles
topics.description: Draw and identify points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines; identify these in two-dimensional figures
evidence: Draw a pair of perpendicular lines and a pair of parallel lines
Identify all pairs of parallel sides in a trapezoid
Mark a right angle, an acute angle, and an obtuse angle in a given figure
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a piece of paper and a ruler, can they draw a line segment, mark a point, and then draw another line through that point that runs perfectly parallel to the first?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring angles
topics.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor; draw given angles and sketch angles of specified measure
evidence: Measure an angle with a protractor and read 47°
Draw an angle of 135° using a protractor
Identify which scale on the protractor to use for an obtuse angle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a protractor and an angle drawn on paper, can they measure it accurately and then draw a new angle of a size you specify?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring angles (age 9+)
topics.description: Recognise angle measure as additive; find unknown angles by adding or subtracting on a diagram using equations with a symbol for the unknown
evidence: Two angles on a straight line are 65° and x°; find x = 115°
An angle is decomposed into 35° and 40°; state the whole angle is 75°
Solve: angles at a point are 120°, 90°, and x°; find x = 150°
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two angles sit next to each other on a straight line and one is 65°, can {{name}} work out the other angle — knowing that angles on a straight line always add up to 180°?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Regular and irregular polygons
topics.description: Distinguish between regular and irregular polygons based on reasoning about equal sides and equal angles
evidence: Classify a set of polygons as regular or irregular
Explain that a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and 5 equal angles
Identify that a rectangle is irregular (equal angles but not all equal sides) unless it is a square
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you show {{name}} a stop sign (regular octagon) and a wonky eight-sided shape, can they explain which is regular and which is irregular — and why?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Transformations on a Grid
topics.description: Identify, describe, and represent the position of a shape following a reflection or translation using appropriate language; know that the shape has not changed
evidence: Reflect a triangle in a vertical mirror line on a coordinate grid and state the new coordinates
Translate a shape 3 units right and 2 units up and describe the movement
Explain that a reflected/translated shape is congruent to the original
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} slides or flips a shape on squared paper, can they describe exactly where it ends up and confirm the shape itself hasn't changed size or angles?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding angles (age 9+)
topics.description: Use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles
evidence: Given one side of a rectangle is 8 cm and the perimeter is 28 cm, find the other side
Explain that all angles in a rectangle are 90°
Find a missing side of a rectangle given its area and one side length
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows one side of a rectangular garden is 7 m, can they tell you the length of the opposite side and all four corner angles — without measuring?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Is an Angle?
topics.description: Understand that an angle is a geometric shape formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint (vertex); recognise angles in real-life contexts and 2-D shapes
evidence: Identify the vertex and arms of an angle in a diagram
Find examples of angles in the classroom (e.g. open door, clock hands)
Explain why two rays meeting at a point form an angle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you draw two lines starting from the same point on paper, can {{name}} tell you that the space between them is an angle — and point to the vertex where they meet?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 2-D shapes (age 10+)
topics.description: Draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles, using a ruler and protractor accurately
evidence: Draw a triangle with sides 5 cm, 7 cm and an included angle of 60°
Construct a rectangle with given length and width using a ruler and set square
Draw a regular pentagon given the side length and interior angle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to draw a triangle with sides of 5 cm and 7 cm with a 40° angle between them, can they use a ruler and protractor to draw it accurately?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 3-D shapes (age 10+)
topics.description: Recognise, describe, and build simple 3-D shapes, including making nets
evidence: Identify which net will fold into a given 3-D shape
Construct the net of a triangular prism and fold it to verify
Describe a 3-D shape by naming its faces, edges, and vertices
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a flat cross-shaped piece of card (a net), can they predict what 3-D shape it will make when folded up — and then fold it to check?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angles in triangles (age 10+)
topics.description: Find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals, and regular polygons using angle sum properties
evidence: Find a missing angle in a triangle given two angles (using angle sum = 180°)
Calculate a missing angle in a quadrilateral (angle sum = 360°)
Calculate the interior angle of a regular hexagon from the angle sum formula
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that angles in a triangle always add up to 180°, and two angles in a triangle are 55° and 70°, can they work out the third angle without measuring it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Classifying shapes by properties
topics.description: Compare and classify geometric shapes based on their properties and sizes; understand that attributes belonging to a category also belong to all subcategories; classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
evidence: Explain why all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares
Place quadrilaterals in a hierarchy diagram showing subset relationships
Identify properties shared by all parallelograms and explain why rhombuses and rectangles are special cases
topics.assessmentPrompt: If someone asks {{name}} "is a square also a rectangle?", can they explain why the answer is yes — because a square has all the properties of a rectangle plus equal sides?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Coordinates (age 10+)
topics.description: Describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants); use coordinates with negative values
evidence: Plot points with negative coordinates such as (−3, 4) and (2, −5) on a four-quadrant grid
Identify the quadrant in which a given point lies
Describe the position of a shape using coordinates in all four quadrants
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is playing a game where ships can be at negative coordinates too, can they correctly plot and read positions like (−3, 2) or (1, −4) on a grid?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Understand a coordinate system defined by two perpendicular number lines (axes) with an origin at (0,0); know that an ordered pair (x, y) specifies a unique point where the first number gives horizontal distance and the second gives vertical distance from the origin
evidence: Identify the x-axis, y-axis, and origin on a coordinate grid
Explain that (3, 5) means go 3 along the x-axis and 5 up the y-axis
Distinguish (2, 4) from (4, 2) by explaining each coordinate's meaning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a map with a grid and you describe a location as "3 across and 5 up from the origin", can they find the exact point — and explain what each of the two numbers tells you?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Parts of a circle
topics.description: Illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter, and circumference; know that the diameter is twice the radius
evidence: Label the radius, diameter, and circumference on a circle diagram
Calculate the diameter given a radius of 4.5 cm (diameter = 9 cm)
Explain the relationship between radius and diameter in their own words
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a round plate and a ruler, can they measure the diameter — and explain how the radius compares to the diameter?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Plotting points in the first quadrant
topics.description: Plot and read ordered pairs in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane; represent real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points and interpreting coordinate values in context
evidence: Plot the point (4, 7) accurately on a first-quadrant grid
Graph a set of data pairs (e.g. time vs distance) as points on the coordinate plane
Read coordinates of a plotted point and explain what they represent in a given scenario
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you tell {{name}} a car journey passes through grid points (2, 3), (5, 7), and (8, 4) on a map, can they plot those points and describe what the journey looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Translating and reflecting shapes
topics.description: Draw and translate simple shapes on the coordinate plane; reflect shapes in the axes
evidence: Translate a triangle 3 units right and 2 units down on a coordinate grid and state the new coordinates
Reflect a shape in the x-axis and list the coordinates of the reflected vertices
Explain how translation changes coordinates (add/subtract) while reflection changes the sign of one coordinate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a triangle at coordinates (1, 2), (3, 2), and (2, 4) on a grid, can they then reflect it across the x-axis and tell you the new coordinates of each corner?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding angles (age 10+)
topics.description: Recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite; find missing angles using these properties
evidence: Find a missing angle at a point given the other angles (total 360°)
Use the straight-line property (angles sum to 180°) to find an unknown angle
Identify vertically opposite angles and use the property that they are equal to find unknowns
topics.assessmentPrompt: If two straight lines cross each other, can {{name}} tell you which pairs of angles are equal (vertically opposite) — and find a missing angle if you give them one of the others?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 3-D shapes (age 11+)
topics.description: Use the properties of faces, surfaces, edges, and vertices of 3-D shapes (cubes, cuboids, prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres) to solve problems, including visualising cross-sections
evidence: Count and describe the faces, edges, and vertices of a triangular prism and a square-based pyramid
Describe the 2-D cross-section produced by slicing a cylinder horizontally or a cone vertically
Use properties of 3-D shapes to determine whether a given net will fold into a specified solid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} slices a cylinder straight across the middle like cutting a tin of beans in half, can they describe the shape of the cut surface? What about slicing at an angle?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angles in triangles (age 11+)
topics.description: Derive and apply formulae for the area of triangles, parallelograms, and trapezia, and for the volume of cuboids and other prisms (including cylinders), connecting each formula to its geometric reasoning
evidence: Calculate the area of a trapezium using A = ½(a + b) × h and explain why the formula works
Find the volume of a triangular prism by calculating cross-sectional area × length
Derive the formula for the volume of a cylinder as π × r² × h by reasoning from the prism formula
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to tile a triangular section of a patio with a base of 4 m and height of 3 m, can they work out the area to know how many tiles to buy?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angle sums in triangles and polygons
topics.description: Derive and use the angle sum in a triangle (180°), use it to deduce the angle sum in any polygon ((n−2) × 180°), and calculate interior and exterior angles of regular polygons
evidence: Calculate a missing angle in a triangle by subtracting the known angles from 180°
Find the sum of interior angles in a hexagon by dividing it into triangles
Calculate each interior and exterior angle of a regular polygon given the number of sides
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°, can they work out the third? And can they figure out the angles inside a regular pentagon?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Coordinate Transformations
topics.description: Identify properties of translations, rotations, and reflections; describe and perform these transformations on given figures, and understand that the image is congruent to the original
evidence: Reflect a shape in a given mirror line (including diagonal lines) and state the coordinates of the image
Rotate a shape about a given centre by 90° or 180° and describe the result
Translate a shape by a given vector and verify that lengths and angles are preserved
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to rotate a triangle 90° clockwise around a fixed point, can they work out where each corner ends up — and confirm the triangle is still the same size and shape?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring angles (age 11+)
topics.description: Draw and measure line segments and angles accurately using ruler and protractor, and interpret scale drawings to extract real measurements
evidence: Draw a triangle accurately given two sides and the included angle (SAS)
Measure angles in a geometric figure to the nearest degree using a protractor
Read a scale drawing to determine actual lengths, explaining the scale used
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an architect's floor plan where 1 cm represents 2 m, can they measure a room on the plan and work out its real-world dimensions?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
topics.description: Derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles using appropriate language, including interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, and relationships between side lengths
evidence: List and verify properties of a parallelogram (opposite sides parallel/equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other)
Explain why a square is a special case of both a rectangle and a rhombus
Derive the relationship between the radius, diameter, and circumference of a circle
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} why the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal in length, can they explain it using the properties of the shape — rather than just measuring to check?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Types of angles (age 11+)
topics.description: Use conventional geometric terms and notation to describe, sketch, and draw points, lines, parallel and perpendicular lines, right angles, regular polygons, and reflectively/rotationally symmetric polygons
evidence: Use correct notation for line segments (AB), angles (∠ABC), and parallel lines (AB ∥ CD)
Sketch a regular hexagon and describe its rotational and reflective symmetry
Identify and label perpendicular and parallel lines in a given figure using standard symbols
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to describe a triangle using proper geometry notation — naming its angles and sides with letters — can they do it clearly enough for someone else to draw it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding angles (age 11+)
topics.description: Apply the properties of angles at a point (360°), on a straight line (180°), and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems
evidence: Find a missing angle using the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180°
Use vertically opposite angles are equal to set up and solve an equation for an unknown
Combine multiple angle facts in a single diagram to find several missing angles step by step
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a diagram with several angles marked at crossing lines and some unknown, can they use the rules about straight lines and crossing lines to find all the missing angles step by step?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angles in triangles (age 12+)
topics.description: Know and use the criteria for triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS), use standard labelling conventions for sides and angles of triangle ABC, and determine whether two triangles are congruent
evidence: State which congruence criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, or RHS) applies to a given pair of triangles
Use the notation △ABC ≅ △DEF and match corresponding sides and angles
Determine whether given measurements produce a unique triangle, more than one, or none
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown two triangles where all three sides of one match all three sides of the other, can they explain why those triangles must be identical in shape and size?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Angles with parallel lines
topics.description: Understand and use the relationship between parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles, alternate interior angles, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles; use these to find unknown angles
evidence: Identify alternate, corresponding, and co-interior angle pairs in a diagram with parallel lines
Explain why alternate angles are equal using the concept of translation along the transversal
Find missing angles in a parallel-line diagram using a combination of angle relationships
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a Z-shape or F-shape formed by two parallel lines and a crossing line in a diagram, can they identify the equal angles and explain why they’re equal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Circles: Circumference & Area
topics.description: Calculate the circumference and area of circles using the formulae C = πd (or 2πr) and A = πr², and solve problems involving perimeters and areas of composite shapes that include circular parts
evidence: Calculate the circumference and area of a circle given its radius or diameter
Find the perimeter or area of a composite shape made from rectangles and semicircles
Explain the relationship between π, diameter, and circumference informally
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to know how far a bicycle wheel travels in one full rotation, can they use the diameter of the wheel and π (pi) to work out the circumference?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Coordinates (age 12+)
topics.description: Understand similarity as a relationship where one shape is an enlargement of another; construct similar shapes by enlargement with a given scale factor and centre, with and without coordinate grids
evidence: Enlarge a shape by a given scale factor from a specified centre of enlargement
Determine the scale factor between two similar shapes by comparing corresponding sides
Explain why corresponding angles in similar shapes are equal while sides are in proportion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to enlarge a photo so it's three times bigger, can they work out the new dimensions — and explain that the shape stays the same but all lengths increase by the same factor?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding angles (age 12+)
topics.description: Use ruler and compasses to perform standard constructions: perpendicular bisector of a line segment, perpendicular to a line from or at a given point, and bisecting an angle
evidence: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment using compasses and a straight edge
Construct an angle bisector and verify by measuring both halves
Construct a perpendicular from a point to a line using compasses only
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has only a ruler and a pair of compasses, can they construct a line that cuts another line segment exactly in half at a right angle — without using a protractor?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Trigonometry basics
topics.description: Use the trigonometric ratios sin, cos, and tan in right-angled triangles to find unknown sides and angles, including setting up the correct ratio for a given problem
evidence: Identify which trigonometric ratio to use (SOH CAH TOA) based on the known and unknown sides
Calculate an unknown side using sin, cos, or tan and a known angle
Find an unknown angle using the inverse trigonometric function (e.g. tan⁻¹)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a ladder is 5 metres long and leans against a wall at 70° to the ground, can they use trigonometry to work out how high up the wall it reaches?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Types of angles (age 13+)
topics.description: Apply Pythagoras’ Theorem (a² + b² = c²) to calculate unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles, including in real-world and coordinate-geometry contexts
evidence: Calculate the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle given the two shorter sides
Find a shorter side given the hypotenuse and the other short side
Use Pythagoras’ Theorem to find the distance between two points on a coordinate grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to check whether a shelf bracket makes a perfect right angle and the sides measure 30 cm, 40 cm, and 50 cm, can they use Pythagoras to verify?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Early Maths Vocabulary
topics.description: Use mathematical words carefully when counting, comparing, and describing shapes and positions
evidence: Use 'more than', 'fewer than', and 'the same as' correctly when comparing groups
Name shapes correctly and describe their features using words like 'sides' and 'corners'
Use positional words (above, below, next to) precisely to describe where objects are
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} talks about maths — like comparing numbers or describing shapes — do they use the right words, like "larger than", "fewer", "beside", or "corner"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding efficient methods
topics.description: Notice when a calculation or pattern repeats and use this to count more efficiently or predict results
evidence: Notice that skip counting by 2s follows a repeating odd/even pattern
Recognise that adding 1 to any number always gives the next counting number
Use a repeated pattern (e.g. +10 on a hundred chart always moves down one row) to predict answers
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is counting or doing repeated additions, have they started to notice the pattern — like "5, 10, 15, 20…" — and used it to predict the next number without counting one by one?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Hands-On Problem Solving
topics.description: Select and use familiar tools (concrete objects, fingers, ten frames) to help solve a mathematical problem
evidence: Choose cubes, counters, or fingers to help solve an addition or subtraction problem
Use a ten frame to organise objects for counting or comparing
Explain why a particular tool (e.g. cubes rather than fingers) was chosen for a given problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is working out a maths problem, do they reach for helpful tools — like using their fingers, counters, or a number line — to support their thinking?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Making Sense of Problems
topics.description: Make sense of a problem by identifying what is being asked, choosing concrete objects or pictures to represent the situation, and explaining a pathway to the solution
evidence: When given a word problem within 10, explain what the problem is asking before attempting to solve
Choose objects, fingers, or drawings to represent a problem situation
After finding an answer, check it makes sense (e.g. re-count objects to verify a total)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} gets a maths problem they don't immediately know how to solve, do they stop and think about what the question is asking — maybe drawing a picture — before diving in?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Real-World to Maths Connections
topics.description: Move between a real-world situation and a mathematical representation using concrete objects, drawings, diagrams, tables, number sentences, or bar models
evidence: Given a story about combining groups, represent it with counters or cubes and find the total
Given a set of objects, tell a simple addition or subtraction story to match
Connect a physical action (putting together, taking away) to the matching operation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is working out a real-life maths problem — like sharing 8 sweets between 2 people — can they use objects or draw a picture to show what's happening before writing any numbers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Showing Your Working
topics.description: Show and tell how a mathematical answer was found using objects, drawings, and spoken words
evidence: Use objects or drawings to demonstrate how an addition or subtraction was solved
Respond to 'how do you know?' by pointing to objects or a drawing and describing what was done
Listen to a peer's explanation and say whether they agree or disagree
topics.assessmentPrompt: After {{name}} solves a maths problem, can they explain how they got their answer — using counters, a drawing, or words — rather than just writing down the final number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Spotting mathematical patterns
topics.description: Notice simple patterns and structures: spot that changing order doesn't change the total, and recognise how numbers relate to each other
evidence: Notice that 3 + 2 gives the same answer as 2 + 3 (early commutativity)
Recognise that teen numbers are 'ten and some more' (e.g. 14 is 10 and 4)
Spot a pattern in a sequence of objects or numbers and predict what comes next
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} noticed that adding numbers in a different order gives the same answer — like 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 both equal 8 — and can they explain why that makes sense?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using objects to model real problems
topics.description: Use objects, drawings, or simple number sentences to represent a real-world situation (early mathematical modelling)
evidence: Draw a picture or use objects to represent a simple real-world situation involving counting or comparing
Write or dictate a number sentence to describe a real-world situation (e.g. 'I had 5 apples and ate 2')
Use the model to answer a question about the situation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you describe a simple real-life situation to {{name}} — like "there are 3 birds on a fence and 2 more land" — can they write a number sentence like 3 + 2 = 5 to represent it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Connecting maths to real life
topics.description: Represent real-world problems with number sentences, bar models, or diagrams, and interpret the mathematical result back in context
evidence: Choose and write an appropriate number sentence for a measurement or money word problem
Draw a bar model or diagram to represent a two-step or comparison problem
Interpret the numerical answer in context (e.g. '15 cm means the ribbon is 15 centimetres long')
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} solves a word problem by drawing a bar model or writing an equation, can they also explain what their answer means in the real-world context — like "that means each child gets 4 sweets"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Connecting Representations
topics.description: Move between real-world situations, drawings, and number sentences, explaining how each representation connects to the others (quantitative reasoning)
evidence: Write a number sentence (e.g. 14 + 5 = 19) to match a word problem and explain the connection
Draw a bar model or part-whole diagram to represent a problem, then solve using the diagram
Translate between a concrete model and a symbolic equation, describing what each number represents
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} solves a word problem, can they draw a diagram or write a number sentence to show their thinking — and then explain how the picture and the numbers match the real situation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
topics.description: With teacher prompting, explain and justify mathematical reasoning using drawings, number sentences, or words
evidence: Explain a solution strategy using a drawing or number sentence (e.g. 'I made ten first, then added the rest')
Justify why an answer is correct by showing an alternative method that gives the same result
Identify and explain an error in a worked example or a peer's solution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} "how did you work that out?", can they show you with a drawing or explain their steps in simple words?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Generalising Patterns
topics.description: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: spot calculation patterns, describe rules for sequences, and predict results using known mathematical facts
evidence: Use a known doubles fact to derive a near-doubles answer (e.g. 6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13)
Notice that subtracting 10 from any two-digit number always reduces the tens digit by 1
Describe a rule for a pattern and use it to extend or predict (e.g. 'each time we add 5, the ones digit alternates between 0 and 5')
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is practising times tables or number patterns, do they spot a shortcut — like "if 6 × 7 = 42, then 6 × 8 must be 48" — and use known facts to work out ones they haven't memorised yet?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Guided Multi-Step Problem Solving
topics.description: With teacher guidance, make sense of multi-step and more complex problems by planning a pathway to the solution, identifying relevant information, and choosing appropriate operations
evidence: When given a word problem within 20 or 100, identify the known information and what needs to be found
Try a strategy (drawing, number line, known fact) and switch approach if the first attempt stalls
Check the reasonableness of an answer using estimation or a different method
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out that 3 children each get 12 sweets and ends up with 5, does {{name}} pause and say "that doesn't seem right" rather than just writing it down?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Select and use appropriate tools and representations (number lines, hundred squares, rulers, part-whole models) to support problem-solving
evidence: Choose a number line or hundred square to support adding or subtracting two-digit numbers
Select a ruler when a problem requires measuring length
Explain why one representation (e.g. a number line vs cubes) is more helpful for a particular problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is tackling a maths problem, do they choose a useful tool — like a number line for addition or a hundred square to count on — rather than always working in their head?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Precise Maths Communication
topics.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary, specify units, and use symbols accurately
evidence: Use the = sign correctly to mean 'is the same as' rather than 'the answer is'
Include units when giving a measurement answer (e.g. '12 cm' not just '12')
